en: Preface to the Record of the Single Transmission of Nanyue.
To examine in detail the Dharma of Śākyamuni throughout the world and for future generations: there is, first, the *zong* (essence/lineage), and second, the *jiao* (teaching).
The *zong* exists so as to clarify the Way; the *jiao* likewise exists so as to clarify the Way. Since Kāśyapa [the Buddha] raised his voice for forty-nine years, he opened...

He expanded the boundaries of the land. Finally, he solemnly entrusted the school of the "Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings" to Venerable Kāśyapa, and commanded Ānanda as his deputy to propagate the transformation.
In succession, through twenty-six generations, they preached the Dharma and saved countless people.

In the exchange of spiritual jabs (*jīfēng*), one may judge by outward appearance; this is the "communication through teaching" (*shuōtōng*). Yet the "eye of the school" (*zōngyǎn*) lies beyond the body of the words;

unless one possesses a mind clearly sealed with the seal of realization, one will not know that this is the "communication of the school" (*zōngtōng*). When the Master of Daruma came from the West bearing the Dharma, the destiny of the Dharma was at a turning point.
As the era changed and the mandate shifted, the true position congealed the imperial decree: it is vast and empty, without a sage; it is not obtained from others, but is Heaven itself.
When the thoroughfares were first opened, the paths of speech were not yet established; when the Great Function manifested before one, no fixed rules should be maintained.

Thus, through five transmissions, the "Miao" people of fierce and sharp faculties emerged, who simultaneously encompassed both the Eastern and Western streams as they flowed together. At Mount Nanyue, the prophecy was fulfilled.
A single colt emerges; suddenly thunder rends the earth and clouds part across the nine heavens. The true vermilion banners and armor are renewed, reaching directly to Dongshan Zhaojue.

His utterances are like knives and saws, entirely the penetration of the source (zongtong). Yet, like snow amidst flames or flowers upon iron seams, they do not prioritize the penetration of doctrine (shuotong), while nevertheless fully embodying the utility of such penetration. Since the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, the Buddha-dharma...

Having entered China, the teaching has been widespread for a long time. Bodhidharma, who came from the West carrying the Dharma, did so because the human mind wanders through the cycles of kalpas without ceasing;
birth and death manifest in every moment. Even the obstruction of principle hinders right knowledge and vision;
what is valued is a single phrase that accords with the truth, entering directly with a single blade. If, however, one continues to rely solely on conventional words and expressions...

If one holds such views in high esteem, what need is there for a "separate transmission outside the teachings"? Those who later attained genuine and clear realization were as vast and expansive as a great ocean;

though their expedient explanations flowed freely, they never failed to cut through the stream. As they were gradually moistened by the sun and year after year by the rain, they forgot that their minds were wandering outward, dazzling themselves with the profusion of the Six Dynasties while remaining ignorant of the embroidered robes of the era of Tang and Yu.
Having borrowed these things for so long without returning them, how could they know they did not truly possess them? Thus, the Dharma was widely propagated.

Chǔ, deeply mindful of the grace and virtue of his predecessors, felt that even the sacrifice of his own body could not repay their kindness. He thus composed the *Record of the Single Transmission of Nanyue* to manifest and propagate it.
His Dharma-heir, Zhù, residing at Nanqian under the domain of Yao, fully embodied his master’s intent; together they planned to restore antiquity and provide salvation for those yet to come.
The Sixty-ninth Patriarch, Shishi Lin, succeeded to the abbotship of Fuyan. He was the dharma heir of Wulingyan Hongchu.
This preface is respectfully composed by [the author]. *Record of the Single Transmission of Nanyue*.

The śramaṇa Hongchu of Lingyan, a successor to the patriarchs at Fuyan Chan Monastery, presents this memorial to the Primordial Ancestor Śākyamuni Buddha (the fourth honored one of the Bhadrakalpa): his clan was Kṣatriya; his father was King Śuddhodana; and his mother was Māyā.
Kṣatriya: Since the renewal of heaven and earth and the initial opening of Jambudvīpa, he has been a king for generations.
Having practiced the path through successive kalpas, he received a prediction from Dīpaṃkara Buddha that he would become a Buddha in this kalpa; subsequently, during the era of Kāśyapa Buddha...
Having attained the Way as a Bodhisattva, he ascended to the Tuṣita Heaven, where he was named the Great Being Mahāprajñāpāramitā (Huming Dashi).

When the time for his manifestation arrived, he descended his spirit into Māyā. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty—the Jia-yin year—he was born from the right side of Māyā.
At the moment of his birth, he emitted the radiance of great wisdom, illuminating the ten [directions].
In the square world, golden lotus flowers sprang up from the earth, spontaneously supporting his two feet.

With one hand pointing to heaven and the other pointing to the earth, he walked seven steps in every direction and looked around the four quarters, saying: "In all that is above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored.
From the time of his birth, various miraculous wonders occurred, as fully described in the sutras. When he reached the age of nineteen, in the second month of the forty-second year...
On the eighth day, wishing to seek renunciation, he thought to himself, "What further encounter shall I have?

He then went out to observe the sights at the four gates and beheld the four conditions of birth, old age, sickness, and death. His heart was moved by both sorrow and joy, and he reflected: "This is old age, sickness, and death."
In the end, he was able to cultivate weary detachment. Then, at the hour of the rat during that night, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens appeared within the window and, with palms joined, said:

"The time for renunciation has arrived; you may depart. Thereupon, the devas supported the hooves of the horse upon which he rode, and he leaped forth into the void, crossing the city wall and departing.
He declared: "I shall not cease the eight sufferings, nor attain unexcelled Bodhi, nor turn the Wheel of Dharma [until my purpose is fulfilled]."

The wheel shall never turn back. King Śuddhodana pondered this deeply and dispatched tens of thousands of his ministers to persuade him to return to the palace, but he remained resolute and did not return.
He entered Mount Taṇḍula to practice the Way; first, at the abode of Ārāḍa Kālāma, he studied the concentration of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" for three years.
Realizing it was not the final truth, he abandoned it. He then went to the abode of Udraka Rāmaputra and studied "the state beyond nothingness" for three years.
He formed a mental resolve; knowing it was not [the way], he abandoned it. Again, he went to Mount Gayāśīrṣa and, together with the various non-Buddhists, ate only hemp and wheat for six years.
The World-Honored One thought to himself: "This asceticism is not the correct liberation. I shall accept food and thereafter attain Buddhahood.
He then bathed in the Nairañjanā River; the heavens caused a tree to lean over for him, and the World-Honored One grasped it.
He emerged and accepted the milk-gruel offered by the daughter of the cowherd clan. He then proceeded to the foot of the *piṇḍapātra* tree.

The Lord of Devas transformed himself into a man who gathered auspicious grass to serve as a seat for him. Auspicious clouds and propitious winds arose from the four quarters, swirling and spreading about.

The celestial Māra thought, "The World-Honored One is about to achieve the Way; I must first suppress him. Leading his hosts, he created obstacles, manifesting every conceivable form of the terrifying and the desirable. The World-Honored One...
He remained serene and unmoving. Pressing the ground with his finger, the earth shook violently and the demons all fell prostrate;
thus he subdued them. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Without mind, thought, or volitional activity, he utterly crushes and subdues all non-Buddhists.

Having first tested them through heterodox methods to demonstrate various skillful means and provoke their divergent views, he led them to Bodhi. This occurred in the third year of King Mu’s reign, the *gui* year...
On the evening of the seventh day of the second month in his thirty-third year, he entered the samādhi of right concentration.
When the morning star appeared on the eighth day, he attained great enlightenment and realized equal and perfect awakening. He then exclaimed: "How marvelous!

All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet because of their deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize it. At that time, he was thirty-three years old.

(Some say that he attained enlightenment on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month; according to the Zhou calendar, this corresponds to the second month, which is the twelfth month of the summer calendar. Six years after his enlightenment, he returned to preach the Dharma for King Śuddhodana.
The king was greatly delighted and dispatched five hundred noble youths of his clan to follow him and leave the household life.

One day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat, and when the great assembly had gathered in order, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said: "Contemplate clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King—the Dharma of the Dharma-King."
"So it is," the World-Honored One said, and he descended from his seat.
Baibiao remarked, "Those who listen to the Dharma with such vivid clarity now shall surely be destined for it. Qian of Yao Feng said, "With every step, one travels ten thousand miles."
The First Patriarch, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, was a native of Magadha. His family name was Brahmin;

his father was named Yinze (Drinking Marsh), and his mother was named Xiangzhi (Fragrant Arrival). In a past life, he was a goldsmith. He encountered the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, at which time the fourfold assembly erected a stūpa.
A poor woman obtained a golden bead and earnestly requested the goldsmith to repair the golden face of the Buddha image within the stūpa.
At that point, they made a vow together: "In every successive life, may we be husband and wife who have never been married before.

By virtue of this cause and condition, for ninety-one kalpas their bodies were all golden in color. In this present life as well, they became husband and wife with the nun Suvarṇaprabhāsā (Golden Light).
The Sanskrit name Kāśyapa means "Drinker of Light" (*pīta-prabhā*), a name derived from the radiance of his body. Nevertheless, both husband and wife lived in pure seclusion. They had no...

Having conceived worldly thoughts, he returned once more to the life of a householder. Later, while practicing the dhūta austerities, a deity in the air addressed him, saying, "A Buddha has appeared in the world;
you should go and take him as your teacher. The Venerable One immediately hastened to pay homage to the World-Honored One at the Veṇuvana Monastery. The Buddha said:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!"—and his beard and hair fell away of their own accord. When the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up a flower to show the multitude.
At that time, the entire assembly remained silent; only the Venerable One broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said:

"I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the subtle and profound Dharma-gate of formlessness within stillness. It does not rely on words and letters; it is the teaching outside the scriptures."
The Separate Tradition. Entrustment to Mahākāśyapa. One day, while the Venerable was treading mud, a śrāmaṇera saw him and asked, "Venerable Sir, why do you do this yourself?
The Venerable replied, "If I do not do it myself, who will do it for me?"

The memorial states: Suppose there were someone who, for eighty full years, provided the four requisites of merit and wisdom to beings within the six realms and four modes of birth across four million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, fulfilling all their desires; yet, after that, one were to give them a single drop of water to drink.
If one does this oneself rather than instructing others to do so, all the previous benefits will utterly vanish. (Signed: Yao Fengqian.
He said: "When the old monks of the world beat the drum and ascend the hall, whether they be seventy-three or eighty-four years of age, each shall come forward and state their name and surname.
The Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda, was a native of Rājagṛha; his surname was Kṣatriya, and his father was King Droṇodana. Thus it truly is.

He was the younger brother of Ānanda. He was widely learned, profoundly enlightened, and possessed unimpeded wisdom. The World-Honored One considered him the foremost among those who possess *dhāraṇī*.
In Sanskrit he is called Ānanda; here it means "Joyous Celebration," a name given because he was born on the day the Tathāgata attained enlightenment.
One day the Venerable One asked Kāśyapa, "Elder brother, besides the golden-threaded *kāṣāya* robe that the World-Honored One transmitted, what else did he transmit?"
"Ma. Kāśyapa called out to Ānanda, and Ānanda responded. Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate!
One day, a certain man said to the Buddha, "Today I entered the city and witnessed a most extraordinary thing. The Buddha asked, "What extraordinary thing did you see?
The man replied, "Upon entering the city, I saw a troupe of musicians performing a dance; upon leaving the city, I saw them all encounter impermanence."
The Buddha said, "Yesterday, when I entered the city, I also witnessed a remarkable sight. The man asked, "I do not know what remarkable sight you saw.
The Buddha replied, "When I entered the city, I saw a group of musicians performing a dance; when I left the city, I also saw musicians performing a dance."
The inscription says: "Where is there even a hair’s breadth lacking? Yao Fengqian said: "Starving, one encounters a royal feast yet cannot eat.
The Third Patriarch, Venerable Śaṇakavāsin, was of the Viśākha clan; his father was Vanavāsin and his mother was Kauśeya-mā.
He was a native of the kingdom of Dhānyakaṭaka. He was born after being in the womb for six years. In Sanskrit he is called Śaṇakavāsa; this means "Naturally Clad.
This is the name of a nine-branch exquisite grass from the Western Regions that emerges whenever a sage is born. When the Venerable One was born, this grass appeared.
Formerly, when the Tathāgata was traveling to convert beings and arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā, he saw a grove of green trees with lush branches and leaves.
He said to Ānanda, "This forest is named Uruvilvā. One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Śāṇakavāsin who shall turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma here.
A hundred years later, Śāṇakavāsin was indeed born; he left the household life, realized the Way, and received the Dharma-eye of the Venerable Ānanda.
Upon arriving at this forest, he subdued two fire-dragons, and the dragons accepted the Three Refuges."

He returned and subsequently donated the land to construct a Buddhist monastery (*brahmapura*). After the Venerable One had transmitted the Dharma, he withdrew into the Śveta-parvata (White Elephant) Mountains south of Kaśmīra.
Later, while in samādhi, he perceived that the followers of Gupta were becoming indolent and arrogant; he therefore went there to correct them.
When Gupta saw the Venerable One arrive and prostrated before him, the Venerable One pointed upward with his right hand. Immediately—
There was fragrant milk pouring down from the sky. He asked Kumāralāta, "Do you recognize this? Kumāralāta could not discern it;
he then entered *samādhi* to observe it, yet still could not discern it. He then inquired, "What kind of *samādhi* is this?
The Venerable One replied, "This is called the Dragon’s Exertion *Samādhi*. You do not know even one of these five hundred *samādhis*. Furthermore...
He said: "The Tathāgata’s samādhi is not known by the pratyekabuddhas; the pratyekabuddha’s samādhi is not known by the arhats;
my teacher Ānanda’s samādhi is not known by me. Now, how could you possibly know my samādhi? This is that samādhi."
The mind is neither born nor extinguished; it abides in the power of great compassion and mutual reverence. Only those who reach this state can truly recognize it.
Thereupon, the disciples of Guptaka all prostrated themselves in repentance and apology. The Venerable One further spoke a verse for them, saying:

"Thoroughly penetrating that there is neither 'self' nor 'other,' The Most Holy have neither long nor short. If you cast away thoughts of contempt and pride, You shall swiftly attain Arhatship. Five hundred [disciples attained realization].
Having heard the verse, the bhikṣus followed the instructions and practiced accordingly; they all attained the state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

[The author] remarks: "Reflecting on these hundred years of physical existence, one need not fear the wind and dew. Yao Fengqian remarked: "I have often seen that hunger and cold fall upon one's descendants."
The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of the kingdom of Takṣaśilā (also named Upagupta, or alternatively Utpalaka). His clan name was Śūdra;
his father was Sumati. He left home at the age of seventeen and realized the fruit [of Arhatship] at twenty. While traveling to propagate the Dharma, he arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā.

Those who attained deliverance were exceedingly numerous. Consequently, the palace of Māra shook violently; Pāpīyān was filled with grief and fear, and he exhausted all his demonic powers to harm the True Dharma.
The Venerable One immediately entered *samādhi* to observe its cause. Pāpīyān again sought an opportunity and took a jeweled necklace to bind the Venerable One’s neck.
Upon emerging from concentration, the Venerable One took the corpses of a human, a dog, and a snake, and transformed them into flower garlands.
He addressed Pāpīyān, saying, "Take this flower garland of mine as payment for your necklace. Pāpīyān was greatly delighted;

he craned his neck to receive it, whereupon it immediately became three corpses, infested with maggots, putrid, and decaying. Though he exhausted all his supernatural powers, he could not remove them.

He then ascended to the six heavens of the desire realm and informed the various celestial lords, and further went to the Brahmā King to seek release. Each of them replied, "O younger brother of the One of Ten Powers..."
"The divine transformations performed by your son—how could we, who are vulgar and lowly, be able to dispel them? Pāpīyas asked, "If that is so, what should be done?

Brahmā said, "You should direct your mind toward the Venerable One, and he will immediately be able to eliminate them. He further showed him this verse: "If one falls upon the ground, one rises from the ground;
to seek to rise apart from the ground is ultimately impossible. Having heard this, Pāpīyas immediately descended from heaven.
He went to the palace where the Venerable One resided, prostrated at his feet, and repented with grief. The Venerable One asked, "From this day forward, will you no longer disturb the Buddha-dharma?
Pāpīyas replied, "I vow to turn toward the path of the Buddha. The Venerable One said, "You may yourself proclaim the taking of refuge in the Triple Gem.
Pāpīyas joined his palms and recited it three times; thereupon, the three corpses were entirely removed. He leaped for joy, paid his respects, and departed.
Biao said, "If swords and blades harm one another, how can one discuss who is at fault? Yao Fengqian replied, "The road back is as winding as a sheep's gut.
The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Tīṣya, was a native of the kingdom of Gāthā. His original name was Xiangzhong.

While Upagupta was in the world providing guidance and instruction, he brought the greatest number of people to the realization of the fruits of the path. Whenever he ordained a single person, he would place a tally-stick in a stone chamber. Of these—
The chamber was eighteen cubits in length and twelve cubits in width, fully occupied [by the monks]. Finally, the Venerable One arrived; he prostrated before Guptaka and requested ordination.
Guptaka asked, "Do you seek ordination with your body, or do you seek ordination with your mind? He replied, "I have come for ordination, not for the sake of body or mind.
Guptaka said, "If it is not for the sake of body or mind, then who is it that seeks ordination? He replied, "As for 'seeking ordination'—"
"The 'house' (family) is so called because it is devoid of self and what belongs to a self. Because it is devoid of self and what belongs to a self, the mind neither arises nor perishes.
That the mind neither arises nor perishes is the eternal Way. The Buddhas are likewise eternal; the mind has no form or appearance, and its essence is the same.

Guṇabhadra said: 'You shall attain great awakening; the mind will spontaneously reach full understanding. You should rely upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha to perpetuate the noble lineage. He then performed his tonsure and ordained him."
Regarding the full ordination: when the Venerable One was born, his father dreamed that a golden sun emerged from the house, illuminating heaven and earth.
Before it stood a great mountain, adorned with various jewels; from the summit of the mountain, a spring gushed forth, flowing in torrents in four directions.
Kuvinda interpreted it for him, saying: "The jewel mountain is my own body. The gushing spring represents the inexhaustibility of the Dharma. The sun emerging from the house is you."
This is now the sign of entering the Way. That which illuminates heaven and earth is the transcendence of your wisdom. For this reason, I shall change your name. In Sanskrit it is called Dīdāga;
in Chinese, it means "Penetrating True Measure" (Tongzhenliang). Upon hearing this, the Venerable One leaped for joy and recited a verse:
"Majestic is the mountain of the seven treasures, From which the spring of wisdom constantly flows. It turns back into the flavor of the true Dharma, Able to deliver all beings from existence."
Regarding this, Kumāralāta also spoke in verse: "The Dharma has been transmitted to you; you shall manifest great wisdom.
Like the golden sun rising from the house, it shall illuminate heaven and earth. The Tathāgata transmitted the treasury of the Great Dharma-Eye in successive order until it reached me.
I now, in turn, entrust it to you. Later, the Venerable One traveled to Central India and transmitted the Dharma to Mīḍhaka. Thus it was said.
Having finished the verse, he leaped into the air and performed the eighteen transformations. Entering the Fire-Light Samādhi (*Jvalana-samādhi*), he spontaneously incinerated his own body.
He inscribed: "In the spring grasses turn green after ten years; longing remains within the square inch of the heart. Qian Yao-feng commented: "At dawn one hears the drums stir;
at dusk one listens to the bells sink into silence."
The Sixth Patriarch, Venerable Mīchaka, was a native of Central India. His country had eight thousand great ṛṣis, of whom the Venerable was the leader.
Upon hearing that Diptaka had arrived, he led his assembly to pay him homage and said to Diptaka, "In the past, we were born together in the Brahma Heaven.
I encountered the ṛṣi Asita, who bestowed upon me the methods of the ṛṣis; you, however, met a disciple of the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha) and practiced [under him]."
"Dhyāna. Since our karmic retributions diverged, six kalpas have already passed. Tīrṭika said, "That we have been separated for so many kalpas is indeed not in vain.
Now you may abandon what is heterodox to return to what is orthodox, thereby entering the Buddha-vehicle.
The Venerable One replied, "In the past, the seer Asita gave me this prophecy: 'Six kalpas hence, you shall encounter a fellow student and attain the fruit of outflowlessness.'"
That we have met now—is this not the result of a karmic affinity from former lives? I pray that the Master will show us compassion and grant us liberation.

Tīrṭika immediately ordained them as monks and commanded the holy ones to bestow the precepts upon them. The remaining immortals had initially given rise to pride, but Tīrṭika manifested great supernatural powers;
thereupon, they all resolved their minds on Bodhi and were ordained at once. Tīrṭika then transmitted the Dharma to them.
A verse was spoken: "Penetrating the mind of the fundamental Dharma, There is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Awakening is the same as not awakening; Without mind, there is also no dharma. Biao said:
"Who can understand the eight arms and three heads? Qian of Yao-feng said: "The peach-spirit talisman has entered the earth."
The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra, was a native of Northern India. He constantly wore pure garments and wandered through the streets and neighborhoods carrying vessels of wine;

sometimes he would chant or whistle, and people called him mad. When Micaka traveled to that country for the sake of conversion, he saw auspicious golden clouds above the city walls and sighed, saying, "This is the breath of a person on the Path. There must surely be a Great Being here."
I, his successor, then entered the city. Amidst the bustling marketplace, I encountered a venerable elder (bhadanta) carrying a vessel of wine.
I went up to him and asked: "From where have you come, Master? Where do you intend to go? Mīṣaka replied: "I have come from my own mind; I wish to go nowhere. The elder asked:
"Do you recognize the object in my hand? Mīṣaka said: "This is a vessel for contact that nevertheless maintains purity."
The Venerable One said, "Teacher, do you recognize me? Mucilinda replied, "I do not recognize you; if I were to recognize you, it would no longer be 'me'.
He further said to him, "Try to state your own name and lineage, and I shall subsequently reveal your original cause. The Venerable One answered with a verse:
"From immeasurable kalpas past, until my birth in this land, My original clan was Bharadvāja, and my name was Vasu."
Madhu. Mīchaka said, "My teacher, Diṅnāga, told me that when the World-Honored One was formerly traveling through North India, he spoke to Ānanda, saying:
'In this country, three hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a holy man whose family name is Bharadvāja.'"
He was named Vasumitra, and among the patriarchs of dhyāna he was destined to be the seventh. The World-Honored One had prophesied of him: "You should leave the household life.
The Venerable One set down his vessel, paid homage to Mithyaka, and standing to one side, said:

"I recall a past kalpa when I once acted as a donor (*dānapati*) and offered a precious throne to a Tathāgata. That Buddha prophesied of me, saying: 'In the Dharma of Śākyamuni during this Bhadrakalpa...'"

He proclaimed the supreme teaching. Now, as the Master of Symbols (Fushi) has spoken, I pray that you grant me deliverance. Mīzhājiā immediately shaved his head and conferred upon him the full precepts.
He then addressed him, saying: "The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is now entrusted to you; do not let it be severed. He then spoke this verse:
"No mind exists that can be attained; What is spoken cannot be called the Dharma. If one realizes that the mind is no-mind, Only then does one understand."
Regarding the mind and mental factors: later, the Venerable Dharmatrāta transmitted the Dharma to Buddhanandi. He immediately entered the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind.
At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and the hosts of devas all came together to pay their respects and spoke this verse: "Ancestral Patriarch of the sages of the Bhadrakalpa."
He occupies the seventh position. Venerable One, have compassion for me and please proclaim the Buddha-ground. The Venerable One arose from samādhi and addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Dharma I have attained is not existent; if one recognizes the Buddha-ground, it is because it is free from existence and non-existence."
Having finished speaking, he returned to samādhi and manifested the signs of nirvāṇa.
He stated: "The great void and the small void. Yao Feng Qian said: "The two taxes upon the common people."
The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhānandi, was a native of the country of Kāmala. His surname was Gautama.

He possessed a fleshly protuberance upon his crown and was endowed with swift and unimpeded eloquence. Just as Vasumitra arrived in the country to propagate the Buddha’s teachings and extensively perform Buddhist rites, the Venerable stood before the Dharma seat and declared, "My name is Buddhānandi; I shall now debate the meaning of the Dharma with you, Master. Vasumitra said:

"O Benevolent One, if one argues, it is not righteousness; if one acts righteously, there is no need for argument. If one intends to argue about righteousness, in the end it will not be a discourse on righteousness.
The Venerable One, knowing that his teacher’s meaning was superior, submitted with reverence and said, "I wish to seek the Way and partake of the flavor of the nectar.
Vāsūmitra then granted him the tonsure and conferred the full precepts, whereupon he spoke this verse: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It manifests as equal to empty space..."
The Dharma of Emptiness. When realizing the nature of space, there is neither "is" nor "is not.

Having transmitted the Dharma of Vajramitra to the Venerable One, he suddenly rose from his seat, manifested great supernormal powers, and then returned to his original seat, remaining solemnly in the state of nirvana.
The Inscription says: "At the Mountain Gate of the Sea, the road to Chang'an stretches vast and boundless; misty waters join with the fragrant grasses. Qian of Yao-feng said:
"I allow you to speak horizontally and vertically; no one shall stop your mouth."
The Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra, was a native of the country of Tika and belonged to the Viśāla clan.
When Buddhadatta arrived at his home, he observed a white light ascending from the roof of the house and said to his disciples, "There is a sage in this household."
His mouth was devoid of speech; he was a true vessel for the Mahāyāna. He did not walk upon the four crossroads, for he knew that contact with them was defiling.
When the elder came out and paid his respects, he asked what it was that [Nandika] required. Nandika said, "I am seeking an attendant.
The elder said, "I have a son named Bhadramitra. He is already fifty years old; his mouth has never spoken, and his feet have never trodden the ground. Nandika said, "If..."
"What you have said makes you truly my disciple. When the Venerable One heard this, he rose immediately to prostrate and spoke in verse:
"Parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin? The Buddhas are not my path; who is the supreme path? Nandi replied with a verse:
"What you say accords with the mind; even parents cannot be compared to it. Your practice accords with the Path; [therefore, you are my true disciple]."
"The mind of all Buddhas is precisely this. To seek outwardly for a Buddha with form is not compatible with you.
If you wish to recognize your own original mind, it is neither joined nor separated. Upon hearing these verses, the Honored One took seven steps.

Nandika said, "This child has encountered Buddhas in the past; his compassionate vows are vast and great. Fearing that his parents' affection would make him difficult to relinquish, he remained silent and did not walk."

The elder then relinquished him and permitted him to go forth into homelessness. Nandiya immediately conferred upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*) and entrusted him with the Dharma, speaking this verse:
"Space has neither interior nor exterior; The nature of the mind is likewise so. If one thoroughly understands space, One penetrates the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Receiving Nandiya’s entrustment, the Venerable One immediately leaped into the air, scattered various precious flowers, and spoke this verse in praise: "My Teacher..."
Among the Chan patriarchs, he shall rightly be ranked eighth; his Dharma transformation will reach immeasurable multitudes, all of whom shall attain Arhatship.
[The Inscription] says: "Had he not been among the commoners who toil at trade, he would surely have wandered aimlessly and alone.
Qian Yuao’s Inscription states: 'I regret that my return was not sooner; I stand solitary before the autumn wind.'"
The surname and clan name of the Tenth Patriarch, Master Xiè, are unknown. He remained in the womb for sixty years.

On the eve of his birth, his mother dreamed that a white elephant carried a precious throne upon which rested a bright pearl; it entered her door, and then he was born. Upon birth, divine light illuminated the room and his body emitted a wondrous fragrance.
Although he grew up eating grain, he was entirely free of any waste or impurities. His original name was Nansheng (Difficult to Be Born). Later, he encountered...
The Ninth Patriarch attended at his side and never slept; because his ribs never touched the mat, he was subsequently titled the Venerable Pārśva.
When the Ninth Patriarch transmitted the Dharma, he spoke this verse: "Ultimate Truth is originally nameless; it is through names that Ultimate Truth is revealed.
Having received the True Dharma, it is neither true nor false. At first, Upagupta traveled to Central India to propagate the teachings. There, the Venerable...
His father, Xiāngài, brought the Venerable One there and, after paying his respects, said, "Once there was a seer who remarked that this child’s physical marks were extraordinary.

Now that we have met you, Venerable One, it would be fitting to let him renounce the world. The Patriarch immediately shaved his head; at the moment of the *karmavācanā*, [the child attained the fruit of Arhatship].
Auspicious light illuminated the seat, and it was moved that thirty-seven grains of śarīra appeared before them.
He remarked: "The mountain has lost its solitary loftiness; the water has forfeited its clear azure. Yao Feng Qian said: "An ancient Buddha reached this point and refused to remain."
The eleventh patriarch, the Venerable Pūrṇāśa, was a native of the country of Puṣpapura. His clan name was Gautama; his father was Ratnakāya.
He had seven sons, of whom the Venerable was the youngest. From childhood, his aspirations differed from those of his elder brothers. He once said:
"If I encounter a Great Being seated at the site of enlightenment, I shall go there to attend upon him and rejoice in his merit. [He traveled] from Central India to the land of the Vatsas.

They came and rested beneath a tree. The Venerable Pindola pointed to the ground with his right hand and addressed the assembly, saying, "When this ground turns golden in color, a holy person shall enter this assembly.
As soon as he had finished speaking, it turned golden. At that time, the Venerable Mahā-Kātyāyana stood before him with palms joined.
The Venerable Upagupta asked, "From where have you come? The Venerable replied, "My mind does not go anywhere. Upagupta then asked, "Where do you dwell?"
The Venerable said, "My mind does not cease. Venerable Xié said, "Are you not settled? The Venerable said, "All Buddhas are likewise so.
Venerable Xié said, "You are not the Buddhas. The Venerable said, "The Buddhas are also not [the Buddhas]."
The inscription says: "Buddhas were fashioned upon excavated roads. Regarding Yao’s bestowal of titles upon the hidden [sages], it says: "On the summit of Mount Xunlù stands the stele of Shen Yu;
its characters are green and the stone is red, the form and pattern being extraordinary."
The twelfth patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, was a native of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. He was also named Saṃgharakṣita;
he was so named because his cultivated and uncultivated merits were preeminent and most excellent.

Pūrṇayaśas’s teachings had benefited immeasurable beings, and those who attained the fruits of realization numbered approximately five hundred. Later, he arrived at the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, where the Venerable One came to attend his assembly.
Pūrṇa said to the assembly, "Do you recognize this one who has come? The Buddha prophesied that the noble Mātr̥ceṭa shall succeed to my Dharma.
Thereupon, the Venerable One paid his respects and asked, "I wish to recognize the Buddha; which one is he?
Pūrṇa replied, "If you wish to recognize the Buddha, it is he who does not recognize. The Venerable One said, "If the Buddha cannot be recognized, how can one know it is he?"
Purna said, "Since I do not recognize the Buddha, how can I know that this is not he? The Venerable One said, "This is the meaning of the saw.
Purna said, "That is the meaning of the wood. Purna asked, "What is the meaning of the saw? The Venerable One said, "It comes out level with you, Master."
The Venerable One then asked, "What is the meaning of 'wood'? Pūrṇa replied, "You have been liberated by me. At these words, the Venerable One attained sudden and clear awakening;
he then requested ordination. Pūrṇa said to the assembly, "This Great Being was formerly the King of Vaiśālī.
Because there was a class of people in his kingdom who were naked like horses, the King exercised his supernatural powers and manifested multiple bodies."
He was raised on silk for his clothing. Later, he was born in Central India. Because a horse-man (a *hayagrīva*) had wept with longing and grief for him, he was named Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Cry).
The Tathāgata had made a prophetic declaration: "Six hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, Aśvaghoṣa will appear in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī;

he shall subdue heterodox paths and deliver immeasurable people. Now is precisely that time. He then transmitted the Dharma, speaking this verse: "Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation."
Light and darkness are inseparable; now I entrust you with the Dharma of concealment and manifestation. It is neither one nor two.
One day, a non-Buddhist seeker challenged the Venerable Master to a debate on doctrine. The King, his ministers, and the fourfold assembly were gathered together at the site of the debate.
The Venerable Master asked, "What is the fundamental tenet of your doctrine? The seeker replied, "Whatever is spoken, I am able to refute it all. The Venerable Master then pointed to the King.
He said, "The present realm is peaceful and secure, and Your Majesty enjoys long life; I request that you destroy this [delusion], so that the heterodox may be subdued.
Baotiao replied, "It is like driving two nails, one above and one below, into the eyes. Yao Fengqian remarked, "It is seven cun long and four cun wide."

The thirteenth patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāla, was a native of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. Initially he was a non-Buddhist teacher with three thousand disciples, well-versed in various heterodox doctrines.
When the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa was turning the sublime wheel of Dharma within the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, an old man suddenly prostrated himself on the ground before him.
Aśvaghoṣa said to the assembly, "This is no ordinary person; there shall surely be extraordinary signs."
Having finished speaking, he vanished. Suddenly, a golden man emerged from the earth, who then transformed into a woman.
She pointed her right hand toward Aśvaghoṣa and spoke this verse: "I bow my head to the Venerable Elder; You shall receive the prophecy of the Tathāgata.
Now, upon this very ground, You shall proclaim and disseminate the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha). Having spoken the verse, she vanished in an instant. Aśvaghoṣa said, "A Māra is about to appear."
"Come! Compete with me in strength. After a short while, wind and rain arrived suddenly, and heaven and earth became dark and gloomy.
The horse neighed, saying, "The arrival of Māra is indeed certain; I shall eliminate him. He then pointed toward the sky, and a great golden dragon appeared, exerting its majestic spiritual power.

The mountains and peaks shook. As Maming sat solemnly upon his seat, the demonic disturbances subsided accordingly. After seven days had passed, a small insect as large as a mosquito appeared, hiding beneath the seat.
Maming took it up with his hand and showed it to the assembly, saying, "This is a transformation conjured by a demon, seeking to eavesdrop upon my Dharma.
He released it to let it go, yet the demon was unable to move it. Maming then addressed [the assembly]:

He said to him, "If you simply take refuge in the Triple Gem, you shall immediately attain supernatural powers and restore your original form. He then resumed his human shape, prostrated, and repented.
Aśvaghoṣa asked, "What is your name? How many followers do you have? The Venerable One replied, "My name is Kambalāśvatara; I have three thousand followers.
Aśvaghoṣa asked, "To what extent can you manifest transformations through your spiritual power? The Venerable One replied:
"I have transformed the vast ocean; that is an extremely minor matter," said Aśvaghoṣa. He asked, "Can you transform the ocean of nature (dharmatā-samudra)?
The Venerable One replied, "What is this 'ocean of nature'? I have never known it. Aśvaghoṣa then explained the ocean of nature for him, saying: "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth..."
All were established upon this foundation; through it, the three samādhis and six supernormal powers were manifested.

Upon hearing these words, the Venerable One conceived faith and, together with three thousand followers, sought ordination. Aśvaghoṣa then summoned five hundred arhats and conferred the full precepts upon them.
He further addressed them, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury shall now be entrusted to you. Listen to these verses. [Hidden]
Manifestation is this very Dharma; light and darkness have been fundamentally non-dual. Now, the Dharma of realization is entrusted: it is neither grasped nor abandoned.
The Venerable One composed the *Nairātmyaparipṛcchā-śāstra* (Treatise on Non-Self) in one hundred verses. Wherever this treatise reaches, there is no place where it does not destroy the Māras.
The Inscription states: "If one discusses this from the perspective of the Reward and Transformation Bodies, others have not yet reached this point. Yao Fengqian said: "The cauldron is cast of iron.
The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, was also named Nāgasena. In his youth, he was able to recite the four Vedas; as he grew older...
He was skilled in all arts and possessed brilliant eloquence and divine insight. Kāpimāra led his disciples to Western India, where there was a crown prince named Meghasvabhāva.
Admiring Kāpimāra’s reputation, the prince invited him into the palace to provide for his needs.
Kāpimāra said, "The Tathāgata has taught that śramaṇas must not associate with kings, ministers, or those of powerful families. The prince said:
"Now, to the north of our kingdom's capital, there is a great mountain. Upon that mountain is a stone cave;
would it be possible for you to practice meditative seclusion there? Māra replied, "So be it. He then entered the mountain and traveled several *li* when he encountered a large python.
Māra walked straight ahead without looking back, and the serpent coiled itself around his body. Māra then bestowed the Three Refuges upon it, and once the serpent had heard them, it departed.
As Māra was about to reach the stone cave, another elderly man emerged dressed in plain garments. He joined his palms in greeting and inquired after his well-being. Māra asked, "Where do you reside?
He replied, "In the past, I was once a bhikṣu who greatly delighted in solitude. However, novice bhikṣus frequently came to seek my instruction;
I grew weary of responding to them and conceived thoughts of anger and resentment. Consequently, at the end of my life, I fell [into this state]."
"I have been in the form of a python, dwelling in this cave for a thousand years. Having just encountered the Venerable One, I was able to hear the teachings of the precepts;
therefore, I have come to express my gratitude. Māra asked, "Are there any other inhabitants living on this mountain? He replied, "Ten li from here," and so forth.

There was a great tree that provided shade for five hundred great nāgas; its king was named Nāgavṛkṣa (Dragon Tree), who constantly preached the Dharma for the assembly of nāgas, whom I too had heard and received from.
Māra then went there with his followers. The Venerable One came out to meet them and said, "This deep mountain is solitary and remote, a dwelling place for nāgas and pythons.
Great Virtue and Supreme Honored One, why have you deigned to trouble your divine feet to come here? Māra replied, "I am not—"
The Honored One came to visit the worthy one. The Venerable One thought silently to himself, "Has this teacher attained the definitive nature and the eye of the clear path?
Is he a great sage who continues the True Vehicle? Māra said, "Though you speak these words in your mind, I already know them in my heart.
Simply prepare for ordination; why worry that I am not a sage? Having heard this, the Venerable One repented and apologized. Māra then conferred the full precepts upon him.
He and five hundred nāgas together received full ordination. In South India, there were five thousand non-Buddhists who employed great illusory arts;
the king and the people followed them in droves, unaware of the Buddha’s presence. The Venerable One was moved by compassion and changed his appearance, wearing white robes and carrying a banner.
Whenever the king went out, he would hasten before him, sometimes concealing himself and sometimes appearing openly. Thus it continued.
This lasted for seven years. One day, the king suddenly found him strange and asked, "Who are you that precedes me as I walk?
I cannot catch up with you, yet even when I let you go, you do not leave. The Venerable One replied, "I am a wise man who knows all phenomena.
The king asked, "Do you know what the devas are doing now? The Venerable One replied, "The devas are currently engaged in battle with the asuras. The king asked, "What [is happening]?"
To clarify this, the Venerable One said, "It shall soon be manifest. Shortly thereafter, spears, halberds, hands, and feet descended from the sky in a chaotic swirl.

The King consequently developed great faith and respect, commanding all the non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) to pay homage to the Venerable One. The Venerable One converted them all, leading them to take refuge in the Triple Gem.
He further composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, and the *Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra*, leaving them for posterity.

The World-Honored One, having entrusted the Dharma to Kāṇadeva, entered the Moon-Disk Samādhi (*candramaṇḍala-samādhi*). He extensively manifested miraculous transformations, then returned to his seat and entered stillness.
After seven days, the heavens rained down relics (*śarīra*). The Venerable One sat upon his seat once more and, pointing toward the sky, addressed the assembly, saying:
"In the past, the disciple of Krakucchanda Buddha, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, made three vows. The first was: 'When I become a Buddha...'"
First, whenever holy beings transform and deliver others, Heaven sends down rain, and their very bodies become śarīras.

Second, all that is produced by the two great earths is fit to serve as medicine to heal the illnesses of sentient beings. Third, all who possess wisdom attain the subtle and profound knowledge of what is known, thereby penetrating their past lives.

The Inscription states: "It is recorded that [this] belongs to the sixth consciousness; it should not be without something to be said. Yao Fengqian remarked: "To speak thus is to address a man who does not penetrate the Dharma.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva, was a native of South India. His secular surname was Viśrāva. Initially...
He sought to cultivate meritorious deeds and also delighted in debate. When Nāgārjuna arrived in South India, the people of that country were mostly devoted to meritorious deeds.

Nāgārjuna preached the Dharma for them, whereupon they said to one another, "For a person who possesses meritorious deeds, there is nothing superior in this world. To speak in vain of 'Buddha-nature'—who can actually perceive it?
Nāgārjuna replied, "If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, you must first eliminate your *asmimāna* (the conceit of 'I'). The people asked, "The Buddha-nature is vast..."
The small tree said, "It is neither large nor small; neither broad nor narrow; without merit and without retribution; neither dying nor being born.
Upon hearing these superior principles, they all returned to their original resolve. The tree then manifested a body of sovereign mastery upon its seat, like the orb of the full moon.
The entire assembly heard only the sound of the Dharma, but did not see the physical form of the Patriarch. Among the crowd, the Venerable One asked them, "Do you recognize this sign?

The assembly replied, "We have never seen it with our eyes; how could we possibly identify it? The Venerable One said, "This is the Venerable One manifesting the essential form of the Buddha-nature to show us.
How do we know this? It is because he has manifested his form through the formless samādhi."

Like the full moon, the meaning of Buddha-nature is vast, empty, and luminous. Having spoken these words, the wheel-mark vanished, and the tree returned to its original seat, whereupon it spoke this verse:
"The body manifests the form of the full moon, To represent the essence of all Buddhas. The teaching of the Dharma has no physical shape, Employed to discern that which is neither sound nor form.
Upon hearing this verse, the assembly suddenly realized non-arising and all vowed to leave the household life in order to seek [enlightenment].
Upon his liberation, the tree immediately shaved his head. He was then commanded by the sages to receive full ordination.

Having received the Buddha’s mind-seal from the Venerable One, he remained concerned that sentient beings would be unable to believe and accept his words. He thereupon addressed the image of Maheśvara, saying:
"May the deity grant me this, so that my words shall not be in vain. Upon arriving at the city of Pāṭaliputra, he heard that various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma.
After reflecting on this for some time, the Venerable One took up a long banner and entered into their assembly. They asked the Venerable One, "Why do you not come forward?
The Venerable One replied, "Why do you not stay behind? They said, "You appear to be a lowly person. The Venerable One [replied]:
He said, "You resemble a noble person. The other asked, "What Dharma do you understand? The Venerable One replied, "You do not understand even one hundred things.
The other said, "I wish to attain Buddhahood. The Venerable One said, "I have certainly attained Buddhahood. The other said, "It is not fitting for you to attain it.
The Venerable One said, "Originally I say that I have attained it; you truly have not attained it. The other said, "Since you have not attained it, why do you say you have? The Venerable One...
The other said, "Because you possess a self, you cannot attain it; since I am without self, I shall naturally attain it.
When his argument was thus refuted, he asked the Venerable One, "What is your name? The Venerable One replied, "My name is Kāṇadeva."
Having previously heard the Venerable’s name, he repented his errors and offered his apologies. At that time, those within the assembly continued to raise various challenges and debates;

the Venerable refuted them with unimpeded eloquence, whereby they were all converted and submitted. In Western India, the use of bells and drums had been prohibited as part of a purge lasting seven days.
The Venerable exercised his supernatural powers, ascended the tower, and struck the bell; thus, the multitude of non-Buddhists—[one...]
At that time, they gathered together and went to the bell tower. Its door was sealed and locked, so they asked, "Who is it that strikes the bell?
The Venerable One replied, "It is Heaven. They asked, "Who is Heaven? The Venerable One replied, "It is I. They asked, "Who is I? The Venerable One replied, "It is you. They asked, "Who is you?"
The Venerable One replied, "A dog. He asked, "Who is the dog? The Venerable One replied, "You. He asked, "Who are you?

The Venerable One replied, "I. He asked, "Who am I? The Venerable One replied, "A deva. Thus they exchanged questions and answers seven times. The assembly of heterodox practitioners realized they had been defeated;
they reported this to the king, who again sounded the bells and drums to greatly propagate the Buddha-dharma.
The Preface states: "I define 'measure' as the various bodies born [into existence]. This differs from the sutras and treatises. Yao Fengqian remarked:
"The river flows with turbulent haste, and the valley winds roar in fury."
The sixteenth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulabhadra, was a native of the kingdom of Kapilavastu. In that kingdom there was an elder named Brahmāśuddha.
One day, mushrooms grew upon the trees in his garden; they were of exquisite flavor. Only the elder and his second son, Rāhulabhadra, took them and ate them.
As soon as they were taken, the mushrooms grew back immediately; once exhausted, they sprouted again. This continued from then on.
None of his other relatives were able to see him. When Kanadeva arrived in the country, he learned of the man's past causes;
he then went to the householder's home. The elder asked him the reason for this, and Kanadeva replied, "In the past, your family once made offerings to a bhikṣu."
However, this bhikṣu’s eye of the Path was not yet clear; because he had unworthily partaken of the offerings of the faithful, his retribution was that of a wooden fungus.
Only you and your son, through diligent cultivation and making offerings, were able to enjoy it. He asked again, "How old is the elder? He replied, "Seventy-nine. Deva then spoke a verse, saying:
"Entering the Path without penetrating its principle, One returns to one's body as a reward for offerings of faith. Your age..."
81. "This tree does not grow [in this place]. Having heard the verse, the elder sighed with even greater admiration and submission, saying:
"I, your disciple, am aged and infirm; I cannot serve you as a teacher. I pray that you accept my youngest son, Rāhulabhadra, so that he may follow you and leave the household life. Deva said:
"In the past, the Tathāgata prophesied that this son would become a great teacher during the second five-hundred-year period. His present marks..."

He encountered [the Master], which accorded with his past causes and conditions. The Master immediately shaved his hair for him. Having received the Dharma, he traveled to the city of Śrāvastī to propagate the teachings.
He then entrusted the Eye of the Dharma to Saṃghanandin, saying in verse: "In this, there is truly nothing to be realized; neither grasping nor abandoning."
The Dharma has no characteristics of existence or non-existence; how could it arise internally or externally?
[The Master] said: "Across the shore there is a mountain, with evening rain stretching across. Yao Feng Qian said: "Why not cut through the white clouds?"
The seventeenth patriarch, Venerable Saṃghanandin, was the son of King Ratnavyuha of Śrāvastī.
From birth he was able to speak and constantly praised the Buddha’s deeds. At the age of seven, he grew weary of worldly pleasures and addressed his parents with this verse:
"I prostrate to my Greatly Compassionate Father; I bow to my Mother of flesh and blood. I now wish to leave the household life; I pray you will have pity on me."

Therefore, his parents firmly tried to stop him. He subsequently fasted for an entire day until they finally permitted him to leave the household life and become a renunciant, giving him the name Saṃghanandin.
They further appointed the śramaṇa Śāṇavāsa as his teacher. For nineteen years, he never once grew weary or indolent.
He would often reflect to himself: "I dwell in a royal palace; why have I left the household life? One night, a divine light descended, and he beheld—
The road was level throughout, and he walked slowly without realizing it. After about ten *li*, he arrived before a great cliff where there was a stone cave;
he took up residence in seclusion within it. Once his father had lost his son, he banished Śrīlāta from the kingdom and went abroad to search for him, but did not know his whereabouts.
When Rāhulabhadra reached the city, there was a river named Suvarṇavāhinī (Golden Water) whose taste was exceptionally fine. In its middle current...
Furthermore, the images of the five Buddhas appeared. Rādhagupta addressed the assembly, saying, "The source of this river is five hundred *li* away;
there dwells the noble Saṃghanandin. One thousand years after the Buddha’s passing, he shall succeed to the holy position.
Having spoken thus, he led the assembly of students upstream. Upon reaching that place, they saw the Venerable One sitting cross-legged in meditative absorption. Rādhagupta...

They waited for him together with the assembly. After twenty-one days had passed, he finally arose from his meditative absorption. Rādhagupta asked, "Is your mind concentrated, or is your body concentrated?
The Venerable One replied, "Both my body and my mind are concentrated. Rādhagupta said, "If both body and mind are concentrated, how can there be inhalation and exhalation?

The Venerable One replied, "Although there is inhalation and exhalation, they do not lose the characteristics of concentration. It is like gold in a well; the essence of the gold remains eternally tranquil."
Rādhagupta said: "If gold is in the well, or if gold has come out of the well, the gold itself is neither moving nor still; what is it that enters and exits? The Venerable One said:
"When you speak of the gold moving or being still, what is it that enters and exits? When you speak of the gold entering or exiting, the gold is neither moving nor still.
Rādhagupta said: "If the gold is in the well, what is the gold that comes out? If the gold has come out of the well, what is the thing that remains inside? The Venerable One said: [As before].
"If gold has come out of the well, that which remains is not gold; if gold is in the well, that which has come out is not the substance. Radha said, "This principle is not so.
The Venerable One said, "That meaning is not adhered to. Radha said, "This meaning must fall away. The Venerable One said:

"That position is not established. Rādha said, "That position is not established; my own position is established. The Venerable One said, "Though my position may be established, the Dharma is not 'mine'.
Rādha said, "My position is already established, for I am without a self (*anātman*). The Venerable One said:
"Because of the non-existence of a self (ātman), what further meaning is established? Rādhagupta replied, "Because of the non-existence of a self, your own position is thereby established.
The Venerable One asked, "Virtuous one, who was your teacher from whom you obtained this realization of non-self? Rādhagupta replied, "My teacher was Kāṇadeva;
through him I realized this non-self. The Venerable One praised him with a verse: "I prostrate to the Teacher Deva, from whom you have emerged. You..."
"Because this [self] is without self, I wish to take you, O virtuous one, as my teacher. Rādha replied in verse: "Since I am already without self, you must see the 'I' within me.
If you would take me as your teacher, know that the 'I' is neither self nor non-self.

The Venerable One’s mind was suddenly enlightened, and he immediately sought ordination and liberation. Rādha said: "Your mind is autonomous; it is not bound by me. Having spoken these words, he then...
With his right hand, he held up a golden bowl and raised it as high as the Brahma palace, taking from there fragrant food to offer as a meal to the great assembly.
However, the assembly suddenly felt revulsion. Rādhagupta said, "This is not my fault; it is your own karma.

He then immediately commanded the Venerable One to share his seat and eat together with him. The assembly was again astonished, and Rādhagupta said, "That you are unable to eat is entirely due to this reason."
"You should know that he who shared his seat with me was the Tathāgata Śālarāja of the past. Out of compassion for sentient beings, he descended to manifest in this world.
You all, during the *bhadrakalpa*, have already attained the third fruit [of the śrāvaka path], yet you have not yet realized the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
The assembly said, "The spiritual power of our Teacher may indeed be trusted. But as for him calling us 'Buddhas of the past,' we harbor secret doubts. The Venerable One [replied]: "Do not doubt it."

He, knowing the pride of sentient beings, said: "In the days when the World-Honored One was present, the world was level and even, without hills or mounds, and without rivers, streams, ditches, or canals;
the water was entirely sweet, the grasses and trees flourished, and the lands were abundant. There were no eight sufferings, and people practiced the ten wholesome paths.
Since his parinirvāṇa beneath the twin trees, more than eight hundred years have passed; the world has become a wasteland, the grasses and trees are withered and parched, and people [lack...]"
His faith was profound, yet his right mindfulness was slight; he did not believe in True Suchness (Tathatā) but cherished only supernatural powers.

Having spoken these words, he gradually extended his right hand into the earth until it reached the limit of the Vajra-wheel, where he drew up nectar-water in a lapis lazuli vessel and brought it to the assembly.

When the great assembly saw this, they immediately felt deep admiration; repenting their transgressions, they prostrated themselves in worship. Thereupon, Rādhagupta commanded the Venerable One to receive the verse of the Dharma-eye.
Hearing this command, the Venerable One respectfully and diligently accepted it, and further spoke a verse of praise, saying:

"Excellent, O Great Sage! Your mind’s clarity surpasses that of the sun and moon. A single ray of light illuminates the world, so that the darkness of Māra is eradicated. [And so it was with the Venerable One.]
After he passed away while clinging to the tree, the arhats wished to move it but were unable to do so; even when they pulled it with the strength of many elephants, it would not budge.
They then cremated him beneath the tree. When his body was consumed, the tree became even more lush and verdant.
Biao said, "We are both monastics; let us not diminish one another. Yao Feng Qian said, "Looking out in all directions, everything is vast and empty—who is there that is not acceptable?
The Eighteenth Patriarch, Venerable Gayasata, was a native of the country of Mathura. His secular surname was Udraka; his father was Tian.

Her mother was then in the state of sanctity; she once dreamed that a great deity held up a mirror, and because of this, she conceived. After seven days, she gave birth; her body was as translucent as lapis lazuli.
She never required washing or bathing, yet she was naturally fragrant and pure. From childhood, she delighted in solitude and quietude, and her speech was unlike that of ordinary children.
When Saṃghanandin arrived in the kingdom to propagate the Dharma, a cool breeze suddenly swept over the hearts and bodies of the multitude, bringing them a sense of joy and comfort beyond compare.
This was constant, yet they did not know why. Nandi said, "This is the wind of the Way and its Virtue.
Surely a Sage shall appear in the world to continue the lamp of the Patriarchs. Having spoken, he used his supernatural power to lead the great assembly through the mountains and valleys.
Within the time it takes to eat a meal, they arrived at the foot of a peak. He said to the assembly, "On this peak there is purple cloud like a canopy; a Sage dwells here."
Thus it was. He then walked back and forth with the great assembly for a long time. The Venerable One, holding a round mirror, went straight before Nandika.
Nandika asked, "How old are you? He replied, "One hundred years. Nandika said, "Your age is still young; why do you say you are one hundred years old?"
The Venerable One said, "I do not understand the principle; I am merely one hundred years old. Nandī said, "Are you skilled in the pivot?

The Venerable One said, "The Buddha said: 'If a person lives for a hundred years without understanding the pivot of all Buddhas, it is not as good as living for a single day and attaining decisive realization.
Nandī said, "What does that which is held in your hand signify? The Venerable One said, "The great perfection-circle of all Buddhas."
A mirror is without flaw or obscuration within or without; two people may see it together, for their eyes and minds are alike.

When the Venerable One’s parents heard these words, they immediately granted him permission to leave the household life. Nandika carried him to his original home, and once he had received full ordination, he was named Gayāśīrṣa.
Hearing the sound of the temple bells being blown by the wind, Nandika asked: "Is it the bells that ring, or is it the wind? The Venerable One replied: [It is the wind.]
He said, "It is not the wind-bells that ring; it is my own mind that rings. Nanti asked, "And who is this mind? The Venerable One replied, "Because both are utterly tranquil.
Nanti said, "Excellent, excellent! Who else but you could continue my Way? He then transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, saying in verse:
"The ground of the mind is fundamentally without birth; The ground arises from conditions. When conditions and seeds do not obstruct one another, The flower..."

The fruit is likewise so. Later, the Venerable Dharmatrāta transmitted it to Kumāralāta. A verse says: When there is a seed and the ground of the mind, Causes and conditions can cause a sprout to emerge.
If the conditions do not obstruct one another, Then that which was to arise will arise; if not, it will not arise.
The Preface states: "One must know that there is a matter of perceiving through signs; otherwise, one merely follows the conventional interpretations of the scriptures. Yao Fengqian said:
"A thousand people pushing against a gate are not as effective as one person pulling it open."
The nineteenth patriarch, Venerable Kumāralata, was the son of a Brahmin from the kingdom of Greater Bactria (Mahā-vṛji). In a former life, he was a deva of the Īśvara heaven.
Upon seeing the jeweled necklaces (*ratnakaṇṭhika*) of a bodhisattva, he suddenly conceived a heart of attachment and fell to be born in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
There, he heard Kauśika preach the *Prajñāpāramitā*. By virtue of that Dharma, he ascended to the Brahma heaven; and because his faculties were sharp, he excelled [in wisdom].
He preached the essentials of the Dharma. The various devas honored him as their teacher, for the time had come to succeed to the lineage. He descended upon the Yuezhi.
When Gayasata arrived at the house, he perceived an extraordinary aura. As he was about to enter, the Venerable One asked, "Whose assembly is this? Gayasata replied:
"He is a disciple of the Buddha. Upon hearing the Buddha's name, his spirit was suddenly stirred, and he immediately closed the door.
Śāṭa knocked on the gate for a long time. The Venerable One said, 'There is no one in this house. Śāṭa asked, 'Who is it that says there is no one?

Hearing these words, the Venerable One knew he was an extraordinary person; he quickly opened the bolt and invited him in. Śāṭa said, 'In the past, the World-Honored One made a prophecy, saying: "After my parinirvāṇa... "
One thousand years hence, a Great Being will appear in the kingdom of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna) to propagate and sustain the profound transformation.
Now you have encountered me; you should seize this auspicious opportunity. Thereupon, the Venerable One developed the knowledge of past lives and devotedly entered the monastic life.

He was conferred full ordination and entrusted with the Dharma. Later, he ordained Jayanta. Once Jayanta had received full ordination, the Venerable One said to him: "The time for my parinirvāṇa has now arrived. You..."

When Daoxiao was carrying out his transformative activities, he transmitted the Eye of the Dharma. He spoke in verse: "In the fundamental nature, there is originally no arising; it is spoken for those who seek it.

Since nothing is attained within the Dharma, why harbor doubts about whether it is resolved or not? He further said, "These are the words of the Tathāgata Wonderful Sound regarding the purity of seeing one's nature.
You should propagate them among future students. Having finished speaking, he immediately used his fingernails to scratch [the surface] upon his seat.
His face was like a blooming red lotus, emitting a great radiance that illuminated the fourfold assembly as he entered nirvana.
Biao said: "To follow this is to turn away from that; to comply with that is to oppose this. Yao Fengqian remarked: "The sun passes and the moon comes;
the wounds and sores [of the world] grow ever more numerous."
The twentieth patriarch, the Venerable Jayata, possessed a wisdom as profound and deep as a vast abyss. When Kumārajīva arrived in the kingdom of Central India, the Venerable One asked him:
"In my family, our parents have long placed their faith in the Triple Gem, yet they are constantly afflicted by chronic illnesses, and whatever undertakings we engage in never turn out as we wish.
Meanwhile, my neighbors, who for a long time have followed the profession of the *caṇḍālas*, are always physically vigorous."
"Kien, your actions were harmonious; what good fortune for him, and what fault of mine? Rada said: 'Why is there any need for doubt?

Furthermore, the retribution for good and evil occurs across three periods of time. Ordinary people merely see that the benevolent die young while the violent live long, or that the rebellious find auspiciousness while the righteous meet with misfortune.'"
He then claimed that cause and effect were lost and that merit and retribution were empty;

yet he did not realize that shadows follow forms and that even a hair’s breadth of action is never mistaken—so that even after passing through hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, it shall never perish. When the Venerable One heard these words, his doubts were instantly dispelled.

Ratna said: "Although you have already placed faith in the three karmas, you have not yet clarified that karma arises from delusion (*kleśa*), delusion exists dependent upon consciousness (*vijñāna*), and consciousness depends upon non-awakening (*avidyā*).
Non-awakening depends upon the mind (*citta*). This mind is fundamentally pure; it is without arising or ceasing, without fabrication, without retribution, and without victory or defeat.
It is utterly tranquil and luminously aware. If you enter this Dharma-gate, you may be equal to all Buddhas."
"It is the same. All things—good and evil, conditioned and unconditioned—are like dreams and illusions.
Upon hearing these words and grasping their meaning, the Venerable One immediately awakened his latent wisdom and earnestly sought ordination.

Radha said, "Where are you from? You must inform your parents before you may leave the home life. The Venerable One replied, "My country is North India, three thousand li from here. However, I have..."
It was a minor artifice; the journey back and forth was likewise easy. He then practiced that art, and together with Rādhagupta, they reached that place in an instant.

When the Venerable One learned of his parents, he bestowed the complete transmission of the Dharma upon Rādhagupta. The King of the Yuezhi, having heard of the Master’s reputation for virtue, [sent an envoy].
He went in person to inquire about the Dharma. Having performed his respects, he requested that [the Venerable] expound it. The Venerable said, "When the Great King arrived, the path was good;
now as you depart, it is just as it was when you came. The King sighed in admiration.
The Inscription says: "Smoke rises from beneath your feet; our two minds are separated by a thousand li. Qian of Yao-feng said: "Bring forth a single phrase in the dead of night!
The twenty-first patriarch, Venerable Po-xiu-pan-tou, was a native of the kingdom of Rājagṛha. His surname was Viśākha. His father...
Guanggai’s mother was the only daughter of a wealthy family, yet she had no son. She prayed at a Buddhist stupa and dreamed that she swallowed two pearls, one bright and one dark;
consequently, she became pregnant. After seven days had passed, an arhat named Xianzhong came to her home, and Guanggai performed a ritual of prostration for him.
The assembly of worthy ones sat upright and received him. When Yan stepped forward to bow, the assembly rose from their seats and said, "We return the greeting to the Great Being of the Dharma-body.
Guanggai was skeptical of this. The assembly said, "Your wife is carrying a holy child; when born, he shall surely become a lamp for the world and a sun of wisdom."
Therefore, I avoided it. However, from a single lactation, two children were born. One was named Vaśiṣṭha, whom I revere; the second was named Cūḍapanthaka.
Formerly, when the Tathāgata was practicing the Way on Mount Himavat, Cūḍapanthaka nested upon his head.
Once the Buddha had attained enlightenment, Cūḍapanthaka received his karmic reward by becoming the King of Nadi. The Buddha prophesied, saying: "When you reach the [seventh]..."
Two hundred and five hundred years later, he was born into the family of Viśākhā in the city of Rājagṛha; he was conceived in the same womb as the Noble One, and now there is no discrepancy.
One month later, two sons were indeed born. When the Venerable One was fifteen years old, he paid homage to the Arhat Prabhāsa and left the household life.
Moved by his devotion, the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin conferred the precepts upon him. When Śāṇakavāsin arrived at Rājagṛha, he propagated the teachings of the sudden (sudden teaching).

At that time, there was a community of disciples who were devoted solely to debate, with the Venerable One at their head. He always ate but one meal a day, never lay down to sleep, and performed prostrations to the Buddha six times daily;
he was pure, free from desire, and a refuge for the multitude. Śāṇakavāsin, wishing to convert him, first asked the assembly:
"Can this Ubhaka-tāpasa, who is able to practice the holy life (brahmacarya), attain the Way of the Buddha? The assembly replied: "He is our teacher."
"Exertion! Why is it not possible? Śāṇakavāsin replied, "Your teacher is far removed from the Way.

Even if he were to practice asceticism for aeons as numerous as dust motes, it would all be the root of falsehood. The assembly asked, "Venerable sir, what virtues do you possess that you should disparage our teacher?
Śāṇakavāsin replied, "I do not seek the Way, nor am I deluded. I do not pay homage to the Buddha, nor do I slight him."
"Arrogance! I do not sit in long meditation, yet I am not indolent. I do not eat but once a day, yet I do not eat at irregular intervals.
I am not contented, yet I am not greedy. My mind has no expectations; this is what is called the Way.
Having heard this, the Venerable One realized the outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and joyfully praised him. Jayanta then said to that assembly, "Do you understand my words? This is why I..."
As for why this is so: it is because his resolve to seek the Way is so earnest. Now, if a string is too tight, it snaps;

therefore, I did not praise him, desiring instead to cause him to abide in the ground of peace and bliss and enter the wisdom of all Buddhas. He further addressed the Venerable One, saying, "I have just rebuked you before the assembly;
was it not distressing to your heart? The Venerable One replied, "I recall that seven kalpas ago, my births were always peaceful and blissful."
The National Teacher [Zhaozhou] was a disciple of Zhizhe Yuejing, who had recorded that I would soon realize the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin.
At that time, a Bodhisattva of Great Radiance appeared in the world; because I was old, I leaned on a staff to pay my respects to him.

The Master rebuked me, saying, "To honor the son and slight the father—how can this be so base? At that moment, I considered myself without fault and requested the Master to point it out to me. The Master said, "When you prostrate..."
The Bodhisattva Mahāprabha leaned his staff against the wall and drew the face of the Buddha. Because of this arrogance, he subsequently lost two fruits of the path.
Since I have taken responsibility for my own faults and repented, even when hearing various evil words, they have been like the wind or an echo.

How much more so now that I have heard the unsurpassed nectar—would I instead give rise to feverish affliction? I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will instruct me with the wondrous Way. Śāṇakavāsin.
Dahui said: "You have long cultivated manifold virtues and shall succeed to my lineage. Listen to this verse of mine: 'In a single word, one accords with the unborn;
it is identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm. If you can understand it thus, you will thoroughly penetrate both phenomena and principle.'"
The inscription says: "Unconsciously, I turned and laughed anew. Qian Yao-feng remarked: "In tailoring the robe, the collar was misplaced.
The twenty-second patriarch, Venerable Maṇḍara, was of the Kṣatriya caste and named Bhaṣu-paṇḍita. While traveling to propagate the Dharma, he arrived at the kingdom of Nādi.
The king’s name was Nityasvayambhū, and he had two sons; the elder was named Mahāra, and the younger was the Venerable One.
The King asked Paṇḍuka, "How does the local custom of Rājagṛha differ from this? Paṇḍuka replied, "In that place, three Buddhas have appeared in the world;
now, in Your Majesty’s kingdom, two masters provide guidance. The King asked, "Who are these two masters? Paṇḍuka replied:
The Buddha prophesied that during the second five-hundred-year period, there would be two great beings of supernatural power who would leave the household life and succeed the Sage.
One was the King’s second son, Maṇḍraka; though my virtue is meager, I too shall be one of them. Formerly, in the kingdom of Nādi, there was a wicked elephant that caused harm;
from the time the Venerable One was born until the harm ceased, thirty years have passed, yet people still do not know it.
Thus they were pacified. Just as the King was conversing with Paṇḍaka at the same table, a messenger suddenly reported that tens of thousands of elephants were pressing against the city walls.

The King was distressed by this, but Paṇḍaka said, "If Your Majesty sends forth your son next, the calamity will be resolved. The King then tested this by ordering the Venerable One to go out. The Venerable One accordingly went south of the city toward the elephants;
