he stroked his belly and let out a great roar, causing the city to tremble and the herd of elephants to fall prostrate. In a moment, they were all...
They dispersed in all directions. It was only then that the people first realized that their thirty years of peace had been due to the Venerable One.

The King developed great reverence and faith, commanding the Venerable One to ordain Pāṇṭhaka according to the tradition. Pāṇṭhaka immediately conferred upon him full ordination and transmitted the Dharma, saying in verse:
"Like bubbles and illusions, they are equally unobstructed; Why do you not awaken to this? To penetrate the Dharma within it— Neither now, nor in antiquity. Thereafter, the Venerable One...
He entrusted this Dharma to Kṣemadatta. Immediately, he leaped into the air and displayed eighteen miraculous transformations.
Returning to his seat, he pointed to the ground, causing a divine spring to gush forth. He then spoke a verse: "The spring of the pure mind-ground can moisten all things;
Gushing forth from the earth, it universally relieves the worlds of the ten directions."

Biao said: "The traveling brothers of today may indeed be believed to have realized the Way; yet the emotional capacity of ordinary people is like unbaked earthen bricks that have not yet passed through the fire.
Yao Fengqian remarked: "When the eighty-four thousand pores open all at once, how many can see through clearly?"

The twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Hòulènná (Haklenā), was a native of the country of Yuezhi. His clan was Brahmin; his father was Qiānshèng (Sahasra-jaya) and his mother was Jīnguāng (Suvarṇaprabhā).
Having prayed to the golden pillar of the Seven Buddhas for a son, she dreamed that atop Mount Sumeru there was a divine child holding a golden ring who said, "I am coming.
When he was born, the heavens rained down flowers. Because there were such divine omens, the King nursed him at the breast.
In the palace, the court ladies raised him. He then manifested his body into as many as a thousand separate sons.
The king said, "I have no heir. I shall raise you all as crown princes. Now that there are a thousand bodies, which one is the true son?
Having spoken, one son emitted a light and suddenly they all vanished, appearing instead in their parents' home. The king could do nothing about it. (7)

In his youth, he observed the profane shrines of the common people; loathing the slaughter performed there, he entered the temples and rebuked them, whereupon the temple images were subsequently destroyed.
His fellow villagers hailed him as the "Holy Child. At the age of twenty-two, he left the household life and dwelt alone in a forest for nine years, reciting the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He was moved by the appearance of a flock of cranes following him. Later, Maṇirata traveled to Western India, where the king’s name was Devaśarman. Gopa... [text fragment ends]
The Dharma family was diligent in serving the Buddha. One day, at the place where they practiced walking meditation, a stupa suddenly appeared, four chi high.

They wished to lift it to offer worship, but though they exhausted the strength of the multitude, they could not move it. The King convened a great assembly of the fourfold community and asked for its origin.
The assembly could not discern it. Maṇḍarava said, "This is the stūpa of King Aśoka; it has appeared because it was moved by the king’s diligent exertion.

The king said, "I venture to ask for the essentials of the Dharma. Maṇḍarava replied, "In the Buddha-dharma, one must be able to fulfill seven matters and eliminate three things before one can study it.
The king asked, "What are these three things and seven matters? Maṇḍarava replied, "The three things to be eliminated are greed, hatred, and delusion."

Delusion. These are the seven qualities he possesses: great compassion, joy, selflessness, valor, benefit for others, subduing Māra, and non-attainment. It is by these that people are either enlightened or not.
Having heard this, the King said, "A Supreme Sage is difficult to encounter, and worldly pleasures are not lasting.
He immediately passed the throne to his crown prince and left the household life. Seven days later, he realized the four fruits of Arhatship. Maṇḍarava added deeply...
He consoled and instructed him, saying: "While you reside in this country, you have skillfully delivered others. Now, there is a great vessel of the Dharma in a foreign land;

I must go there to transform them. Dedu replied: "The Master’s traces reach throughout the ten directions; when you stir a thought, you shall arrive. Why trouble yourself to go? Māṭhara said: "It is so.
Thereupon, he burned incense and spoke from afar to the Venerable One of the Yuezhi country: "You are instructing the flock of cranes."
"The fruit of the Path is about to be realized; you should know this for yourself.
Then, as the Venerable One was reciting a sūtra verse for King Ratnamudrā, he suddenly beheld a wondrous fragrance forming into a cluster. The King asked, "What omen is this?

He replied, "The Venerable Mañjuśrī from the land of Aparāntaka is about to arrive; this is the fragrant herald of his arrival. The King and the Venerable One both turned toward the west and paid homage. Mañjuśrī...
He also used his hand to face east and made three dots on the ground in response. [The king] then took his leave and received ordination.

Together with his attendants, he traveled through the air to the kingdom of Mo-chi (Mūlasthāna). There, the Venerable One and Baoyin (Ratnamudrā) went to welcome Madhyāntika to the royal palace, where he was provided with offerings.
On another day, the Venerable One asked Māṇava: "I have resided in the forest for nine white years.
I have a disciple named Nāgaputra, who was intelligent from childhood; though I have investigated his origins throughout the three periods of time, I cannot know his root.
Māṇava replied: "In the fifth kalpa, this boy was born into a brahmin family in the Land of Wondrous Joy (Abhirati). He once [offered] sandalwood..."
Because he struck the bell at a Buddhist monastery, he received the retribution of being exceptionally intelligent and was held in high esteem by the multitude.
Again, [the King] asked, "By what conditions did I attract this flock of cranes? Māra said, "During the fourth kalpa, you were once a bhikṣu.
When you were about to go to a gathering at the Dragon Palace, all your disciples wished to follow you. You looked among your five hundred followers and saw that not one..."

The man was worthy of receiving sublime offerings. At that time, the disciples said, "Our teacher once preached the Dharma, saying that those who are equal in regard to food are also equal in regard to the Dharma.

Now, since this is not the case, how can he be considered a sage? You have immediately ordered him to attend the assembly; because he ate indiscriminately for this reason, his retribution has been as a bird.
He followed his master due to their past karmic affinity; therefore, why does he now follow [you]? The Venerable One replied, "By what skillful means can I cause him..."
"Emancipation. Mañjuśrī said, "I possess the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure; you should listen and receive it, so as to transform beings until the end of the future.

He then spoke this verse: "The mind turns following the myriad objects; where it turns, it can indeed be profound. If one recognizes one's nature while following the flow, there is neither joy nor sorrow.
Upon hearing the verse, the flock of cranes flew away, crying out. The Venerable One attained the Dharma at thirty and practiced it.
He traveled to Central India and preached the Dharma for King Abhayasāgara. Moved by this, the Sun and Moon Devas prostrated before him.
When the king saw this with his own eyes, he asked the Venerable One: "How many lands of the sun and moon are there in total? The Venerable One replied:
"In each world-system transformed by a thousand Śākyamunis, there are ten billion Mount Merus, suns, and moons. If I were to explain it extensively..."
Thus, it could not be fully described. When the King heard this, he was filled with joy.
[Daobiao] said: "Coming from the place of enlightenment, going to the place of enlightenment—what world is there that has no day or night?
Yao Fengqian said: "To transform a wasteland of rubble into a palace for Brahmā, Śakra, and the devas of the dragon-heavens is far superior to mere peddling."
The Tathāgata was different.
The twenty-fourth patriarch, the Venerable Siṃhabhadra Bhikṣu, was a native of Central India. His family name was Brāhmaṇa. He was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory.
He served as a Brāhmaṇa priest. He had a younger brother named Nāgaputra, who was a chief disciple of the Venerable Haklena; he died young.
When they were about to bury the dragon’s son, the multitude exerted all their strength to lift his coffin, but it would not move.

Helunna said to the Venerable One, "Formerly, when your younger brother wished to provide for your merit in the afterlife, he fashioned a Buddha image. Yet you, believing instead in the Brahmins, cast it to the ground."
"Now, although your younger brother has passed away, I still wish to bring you to realization; therefore, I have manifested this marvel.
If you quickly make offerings to the image, the coffin shall rise. The Venerable One followed these instructions and the coffin rose.
Shortly thereafter, his Brahmin teacher died, so the Venerable One took refuge with Huike (Hegelena) and asked: "I wish to seek the Way; how should I apply my mind? Huike said: "You..."
He sought the Way but had no application of mind. [The other] asked, "If there is no application of mind, who performs the Buddha-work?
Helian said, "If you have any application, it is not merit; if you have no action, that is itself the Buddha-work. As the sutra says:
"Regarding the merit I have performed, I have no sense of 'mine'. Upon hearing these words, the Venerable One immediately entered the Buddha-wisdom. At that time, Helian...
Huileng suddenly pointed toward the northeast and asked, "What kind of phenomenon is this?
The Venerable One replied, "I see a vapor like a white rainbow piercing through heaven and earth, with five black streaks of vapor stretching horizontally across its center.
Huileng asked, "What does this omen portend? He replied, "It cannot be known. Huileng said, "Fifty years after my passing, in the north..."
"In the land of Zhuguo (India), difficulties shall arise; they shall cling to your person. When I have passed away, I now entrust the Dharma-eye to you.
Guard and uphold it well. He then spoke a verse, saying: "When one recognizes the nature of mind, it can be called inconceivable."

"Thoroughly understood, there is nothing to be attained; when attained, one does not speak of knowing. Upon hearing this verse, the Venerable One was filled with joy and satisfaction, yet he did not yet understand what kind of hardship he was about to encounter.
Haklenā then revealed it to him in secret. Having received the Dharma, the Venerable One traveled to various regions until he reached the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
There was a śramaṇa named Pālika who had originally practiced the dhyāna-vision of the Hīnayāna. He had five disciples:

one called "Dhyāna-concentration," one called "Knowledge-and-insight," one called "Grasping at signs," one called "Abandoning signs," and one called "Silence. The Venerable One addressed the one who maintained silence, saying:
In the Buddha’s teaching, one diligently cultivates *prajñā*. Who would not speak thus, yet instead contradict the Buddha’s words? To those who advocate "abandoning characteristics," one says:

"The Buddha’s teachings are fully endowed with dignified deportment and his holy life (*brahmacarya*) is pure; how could this be 'abandoning characteristics'? To those who cling to "characteristics," one says:

"The Buddha-lands are pure, sovereign, and unattached; why do you cling to characteristics? To those who speak of "knowledge and vision," one says: "This refers to the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas."
Because there is nothing to be attained, this Dharma is subtle and wondrous; it is beyond the reach of seeing or hearing. Being unconditioned and signless, how can it be known or seen?

The fourfold assembly was all in agreement, except for the meditation master Dharmadatta. Hearing that the fourfold assembly had been defeated in argument, he came in a state of indignation and frustration.
The Venerable One said, "O worthy one, you practice meditative concentration; why have you come here? Now that you have arrived, why do you say you practice [meditation]?"
[The monk] said, "Although I have come here, my mind remains undisturbed. Concentration follows one's habitual practice; how could it depend on the location?
The Venerable said, "Since you, O worthy one, have arrived, your habitual practice has also arrived. Since there is no fixed location, how could it depend on habitual practice? He replied:

"It is because the person practices concentration, not that concentration practices the person. When I come here, it is because I have constantly practiced that concentration. The Venerable One said, "It is not that the person practices concentration;
rather, it is because the person practices concentration that they will come here of their own accord. When they come, who is it that practices the concentration?

He replied, "Just as a pure, bright pearl has no obscurations inside or out, if concentration is fully realized, it must necessarily be like this. The Venerable One said, "If concentration is fully realized..."

"It is just like a bright pearl. Now that I see you, O Virtuous One, you are not of the sort of person for whom it is a pearl. He said, "That pearl is transparent and luminous; both inside and out it is entirely settled.
My mind is undisturbed, just as this [pearl] is pure. The Venerable One said, "That pearl has no interior or exterior; how can you, O Virtuous One, be settled?
Impure things are not subject to agitation; this 'settledness' is not true purity. Having heard this, Dharmadatta then composed [a verse].
Lǐ said, "In my study of the Way, I have merely labored in vain. Venerable Sir, I pray that you will deign to instruct me. He entreated him with earnest sincerity.
The Venerable One replied, "In the meditative concentrations of the Buddhas, there is nothing to be attained; in the awakened Way of the Buddhas, there is nothing to be realized."

There is nothing to be attained and nothing to be realized; this is true liberation. Regarding the repayment of causes and the answering of effects through worldly karmic retribution, within this Dharma, none of these apply.
Having received the instruction of the Venerable One, Dharmada’s mind became clear and radiant. Once the Venerable One had gathered the fivefold assembly, his fame spread far and wide.
He secretly entrusted the *saṃghāṭī* robe to Sthavira, charging him to go to another country and act according to the needs of the occasion.
Evolution. Sthiramati received many teachings and traveled directly to the Southern Heavens. A venerable master said, "It is impossible to evade this calamity;
you must remain alone in Kaśmīra. At that time, there were two non-Buddhists in his native land named Māmuta and Durlabha.
Having studied various magical arts, they plotted together to incite a rebellion. Disguised as Śākyaputrīyas, they secretly entered the royal palace. Their King—
Mīlāraju then destroyed the teachings of the Śākya and, grasping a sword, approached the Venerable One and asked, "Has the Master attained the emptiness of the aggregates?

The Venerable One replied, "I have already attained the emptiness of the aggregates. The King asked, "Have you escaped birth and death? The Venerable One replied, "I have already escaped birth and death."
The king said, "Since you have transcended birth and death, you may give me your head. The Venerable One replied, "This body is not mine; why should I begrudge my head?
The king then brandished his blade and severed the Venerable One's head. White milk gushed forth to a height of several feet.
The king’s right arm then also fell to the ground, and he died seven days later. Crown Prince Prabhāvatī sighed and said, "For what reason did my father take this upon himself?"
The calamity spread; the assembly performed repentance. At that time, there was a rishi on Mount Elephant White who had a profound understanding of cause and effect.
He said, "The Venerable One and Rāhula were both laymen in a previous life. Because they envied the excellence of the Dharma, they secretly harmed Rāhula; now he must repay that debt.
Thereupon, the assembly constructed a stupa for the Venerable One’s remains.
Biao said, "With earnest and sincere devotion day and night, those of later generations and beginners have doubts and ask questions. Yao Feng Qian says:
'In which kalpa were there no ancestral teachers?'"
The twenty-fifth patriarch, Vasiṣṭha, was a native of Kaśmīra. He was of Brahmin lineage; his father was named Śāntacara and his mother Nityasukhā.
While pregnant, his mother dreamed that she obtained a divine sword. Upon his birth, he held his left hand in a fist. At that time, Bhikṣu Siṃha was seeking a successor to the Dharma.
He encountered the elder Śāntacara and, leading him to the venerable one, asked: "This child’s name is Sthira. He shall be born [as the successor]."
He then clenched his left hand; at the age of twenty, he was ultimately unable to open it. He requested that the Venerable One reveal its past cause.
When Siṃha saw this, he immediately took the fist with his own hand and said, "Give me back my pearl. The Venerable One quickly opened his hand and presented the pearl.
The assembly was all struck with wonder. Siṃha said, "In my previous life as a monk, there was a boy named Vatsa.

Once, when I went to a feast by the Western Sea, I received a pearl as an offering and entrusted it to him. That he now returns my pearl is only natural. The elder then caused him to leave the household life.
At the assembly where the holy ones conferred full ordination upon him, because of his former connection, he was named Vatsasīta. Master...

The Master then said to him: "My teacher has secretly left behind a written record. It will not be long before he encounters peril. The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye shall now be entrusted to you.
You must protect it and universally moisten all beings until the end of time. He spoke in verse: "When the true teaching of knowledge and vision is proclaimed,"
Cognition and vision are both the mind; when the mind arises, there is cognition and vision. Cognition and vision exist right now.

Having attained the Dharma, the Venerable One later traveled to Central India. King Kaniṣka offered him respectful worship and support. There was a non-Buddhist teacher named Nirgrantha who had previously been honored by the king with similar respect.
He then sought to prevail in a debate before the king and said to the Venerable One: "I understand silence."
The Master said, "Without relying on verbal expression. The Venerable One asked, "Who then knows victory or defeat? He replied, "I do not contend for victory or defeat; I seek only its meaning.

The Venerable One asked, "What do you take to be that meaning? He replied, "To be without mind is the meaning. The Venerable One asked, "Since you are already without mind, how can you attain the meaning?
He replied, "When I speak of being without mind, it is designated as such, but it is not a 'meaning' [in the conventional sense]. The Venerable One said:
“You say ‘no mind’; this should be called a non-meaning. I say ‘not mind’; this should be taken as a meaning, not a name.
He said, “If it is a meaning, not a name, who is able to discern that meaning? The Venerable One said, “Your ‘name’ is a non-meaning. What kind of name is this?

He said, “It is for the purpose of discerning what is not a meaning; thus it is called a ‘nameless name. The Venerable One said, “Since the name is already not a name, the meaning is also not a meaning. Who is the one who discerns?”
This is the name. One should now distinguish what object it refers to. In this manner, they engaged in debate fifty-nine times back and forth.

The non-Buddhists were silenced and submitted with faith. The Venerable One is also named Bharadvāja, and also named Bharadvāra. These two names, translated into Chinese, mean "Separate-Action Spring-Multitude.
Regarding the first [name], within the royal garden of India there was a spring whose water was so hot that it could not be touched. King Kṛkin...
He questioned the Venerable One. The Venerable One replied, "There are three causes for hot springs: first, hot stones beneath; second, the karma of ghosts;

and third, the karma of deities. This is due to the karma of a deity. Because [the devotee] had offered incense by the spring and performed repentance on their behalf, after a short while, a deity appeared.
He thanked him for his deliverance. After seven days, the spring became clear and cool, just as it was before.
For this reason, Central India and Northern India both referred to him by two names. Later, he transmitted the Dharma to Ratnamati. Ratnamati asked, "May the robe be passed down?"

The Venerable One said: "This robe was used as a provisional means of verification because of the hardships [of the times]. Your person is free from hardship; your transformative influence pervades the ten directions—why should you rely on the transmission of a robe?"
The Inscription states: "If it were not ultimate, I would not have given it to the Acharya. Yao Fengqian remarked: "One must not hold the views and interpretations of a novice monk or practitioner.
The twenty-sixth patriarch, Venerable Amṛtodana, was of the Kṣatriya caste and was a prince from South India. Po...
Śeṣṭa traveled to Southern India and lived in seclusion within the mountain valleys. King Devaśrī invited him there to provide offerings. The king had two sons:
the elder was named Guṇajaya, who was fierce and violent yet possessed great physical vigor; the younger was the Venerable One, who was gentle and mild but constantly afflicted by illness.
The king questioned Śeṣṭa, who explained the matter in terms of cause and effect. The king received this with reverence and faith. There was also a master of incantations.
Śīta placed poison in his food. Śīta knew of it and ate it, yet he himself was poisoned in return. Consequently, he renounced the world and entered the monastic life under Śīta.
Sixty years later, King Devasena ascended the throne; being deluded by the teachings of non-Buddhist heretics, he interrogated Śīta, saying:
Venerable Siṃha had already encountered the peril posed by the King of Kaśmīra; for what reason, then, did he transmit the Dharma?

This multitude [of relics] was produced from the saṃghāṭī robe transmitted by Venerable Siṃha. When Vasu showed them to Śaṅkara, Śaṅkara ordered them to be burned. Five-colored light issued from the robes, and though the fuel was consumed, they remained as they were.
Śaṅkara then felt remorse and paid his respects. Previously, when Śaṅkara wished to suppress Vasu, the Venerable One went to admonish him, but because of that, [Vasu] was imprisoned.
When it came time for him to depart, he sent the Venerable One out. The Venerable One then requested ordination.
Sthavira asked, "If you wish to leave the household life, for what purpose do you do so? The Venerable One replied, "If I leave the household life, I shall not be for that purpose.
Sthavira asked, "Not for what purpose? The Venerable One replied, "Not for worldly affairs. Sthavira asked, "Then for what purpose will you be? The Venerable One replied:
He thought, "This must be a Buddha-work. Sudarśana said, "The Prince’s wisdom is as sublime as the heavens;

this must surely be the descent of the various sages. He was immediately ordained and left the household life. He attended upon Sudarśana for six years. Later, he received full ordination within the royal palace; at the moment of the *karmavācanā*, the great earth shook violently.

Thereupon, the Dharma was entrusted to him with this verse: "The Sages have taught that knowledge and vision are such that, regarding the objective realm, there is neither right nor wrong. I have now realized the Truth."
In essence, there is neither the Way nor principle. After the Venerable One attained the Dharma, he went to Eastern India.
Its king was Sthira, who venerated the non-Buddhist teacher, the Brahmin Dīrghanakha. When the Venerable One arrived, the king asked, "For what purpose have you come, Master?

He replied, "I have come to deliver sentient beings. The king asked, "By what method do you deliver them? He replied, "I deliver each according to their own kind. Thereupon, the Brahmin transformed himself...
A great mountain descended with great force upon the head of the Venerable One. The Venerable One pointed at it, and the mountain suddenly shifted to rest upon the heads of that assembly.
Again, he pressed down upon the earth with his hand; the earth shook, and the five hundred non-Buddhist practitioners were unable to remain standing.

The Brahmins, terrified, prostrated themselves in repentance. The Venerable One again pressed down upon the earth, and it became still; he pointed at the mountain, and it vanished. On another day, the King [asked] greatly...
For the purification rite (*śuddhika*), he gathered the various non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) and earnestly requested that the Venerable One attend the assembly.

Initially, the Venerable One was unwilling to go, but knowing that the ground where the assembly was to be held would soon collapse, he nevertheless proceeded. The King said, "Master, have you consented to come? The Venerable One replied, "I am not here to receive offerings; I have come to save [the people] from death.
This place has already become a dragon's lair; in a moment it will sink down. The King became terrified and, together with his retinue, [departed].
Upon the high plateau, he looked back at the ground; it had already become a deep, tranquil pool. The King’s reverence and faith increased further.

The Venerable One expounded the Dharma for him, then took his leave of the King, saying: "My work of transformation is now complete; I shall return to nirvana. May Your Majesty not forget to provide external protection for the Supreme Vehicle.
He then returned to his original seat, manifesting a form like the sun.
Biao said, "It is truly a cause for celebration that you brothers may dwell together in the forests and springs with your dharma companions to chew upon this matter.
Yao Feng Qian said, "At ninety thousand li, the wind descends indeed."
The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, was a native of Eastern India and the son of a Brahmin.
Having lost both parents in his youth, he did not know his name or lineage; he sometimes referred to himself as "Hāra" (Necklace), so people subsequently called him the "Boy Hāra.

As he wandered for alms through the villages and neighborhoods, if someone asked, "Why do you walk so hurriedly? he would immediately reply, "Why do you walk so slowly? If asked what his surname was, he would likewise respond.
He shares the same clan name as you, yet no one can fathom him. Initially, when Ratnamati was expounding the Dharma in the kingdom, he said to the king:
"In Your Majesty’s kingdom there is a holy man who shall succeed to my Dharma. One day, the king and Ratnamati were traveling out together in the same carriage.
The Venerable One prostrated before him, and Ratnamati asked, "Do you remember past events? The Venerable One replied, "I..."
He recalled that in a past kalpa, he had lived together with his teacher; while the teacher expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, he himself had expounded the profound *Sūtras*.
That which occurred today was surely in accord with their former causes. Guṇamati looked at the king and said, "This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Hereafter, two persons shall appear: one will transform the southern region of India, and the other’s karmic conditions lie in China for nine years."
He returned to this region and, because of his past causes, was named Prajñātāra. The verse of the transmission of the Dharma says:
"The treasury of the true nature of the mind has neither beginning nor end; responding to conditions to transform sentient beings, it is expediently called 'Wisdom' (Jñāna).
Later, while the Venerable One was invited by the King of Eastern India for a meal, the King asked: "Everyone here recites the scriptures; what does the Master [recite]?"

"Why alone do you not turn [the wheel]? The Venerable One replied, "This poor monk does not follow external conditions with his exhalation, nor does he dwell within the aggregates or realms with his inhalation.
He constantly turns such a sūtra as this—hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of scrolls, not merely one or two scrolls."

The Inscription states: "Profoundly deep, it has no bottom; shallowly shallow, it has no source. Yao Feng Qian says: "It shines peripherally upon the three worlds and shines directly upon the four worlds."
The Great Master Bodhidharma, the twenty-eighth patriarch, was the third son of King Xiangzhi of South India.
His clan name was Kṣatriya, and his original name was Bodhitāra. After Venerable Prajñātāra attained the Dharma, [he was named Bodhidharma].
He arrived in South India, where King Gandhāra honored him with offerings and bestowed upon him a priceless jewel. The king had three sons:
Candravimala, Guṇavimala, and Bodhivimala. Desiring to test what they had attained, the Venerable One took the bestowed jewel and asked the three princes:
"This jewel is perfectly round and luminous; is there anyone who can equal it? Candra...
Jing Gongde said, "This pearl is the most honored among the seven treasures; truly, there is nothing that surpasses it. Zu said, "This is a worldly pearl;
it is not sufficient to be considered supreme. Among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme. This is worldly light; it is not sufficient to be considered supreme.
Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme. This is worldly clarity; it is not sufficient to be considered supreme. Among all forms of clarity..."

Among these, the clarity of the mind is supreme. This jewel’s radiance cannot illuminate itself; it must rely upon the light of wisdom to discern it. Once it has been discerned, one knows it to be a jewel.
Once known to be a jewel, its preciousness is revealed. If its preciousness were inherent in the jewel, the jewel would not be precious by itself.
If its quality as a jewel were inherent in the jewel, the jewel would not be a jewel by itself. That the jewel is not a jewel by itself means that it must rely upon...
"The Wisdom-Jewel. [The Master] then distinguished the worldly jewel. "A treasure is not a treasure in itself; it must rely upon the treasure of wisdom to illuminate the treasure of the Dharma.
Thus, when the teacher possesses the Way, that treasure immediately manifests; likewise, when sentient beings possess the Way, their treasure does so as well.
The Venerable One praised his eloquence and wisdom, and then asked again: "Among all things, what thing is without marks? [He] replied: "Among all things..."
He did not give rise to the markless. Again he asked, "Among all things, which is the highest? He replied, "Among all things, the person-self (*pudgala-ātman*) is the highest.
Again he asked, "Among all things, which is the greatest? He replied, "Among all things, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the greatest.
The Venerable One, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, remained silent and mingled with the crowd as the time had not yet arrived. When [the time for] incense...
When the King grew weary of the world, the multitude all wailed and fainted; only Bodhidhara entered meditative absorption before the coffin and emerged after seven days.
He then sought ordination from the Venerable One, received full precepts, and attained the Dharma.

The Venerable One said to him, "Regarding all dharmas, you have already attained mastery. Since 'Dharma' carries the meaning of 'mastery,' you should be named Dharmatrāta. Consequently, his name was changed.
Now, as for the name: Zu Gong received the teachings and their meaning, serving with diligence for forty years. When the Venerable One passed away, he went to propagate the Dharma in his own country.
His transformation reached the Southern Heavens, and his fame spread throughout the Five Indias. After sixty years, he had delivered immeasurable multitudes.

Thinking of the land of Eastern Zhendan, he recalled the Buddha’s prophecy that during the final five hundred years, the lamp of Prajñā wisdom would cast its light there; thus, he entrusted his disciples.
Puṇyamitra remained in India to transmit the Dharma rather than coming personally to China. He then took leave of the Patriarch’s stupa and his fellow students, saying to the King:
"Diligently cultivate pure deeds; I shall return in nineteen years. The Patriarch then set sail across the vast ocean.

After three full cycles of winter and summer, he reached the South Sea. This was indeed on the twenty-first day of the ninth month in the seventh year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, the Gengzi year.
Xiao Ang, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, received him with full ceremonial rites and provided offerings, reporting the matter to Emperor Wu.
The Emperor dispatched an envoy bearing an imperial decree to invite him, arriving in Jinling on the first day of the tenth month. The Emperor asked: "I am about to..."
Since ascending the throne, he has built temples, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks beyond counting. "What merit does this bring? the Patriarch asked.
The Emperor replied, "There is no merit. The Emperor asked, "Why is there no merit? The Patriarch said, "These are merely the minor fruits of the realms of humans and devas;
they are causes subject to outflows (āsrava). Like a shadow following a form, though they exist, they are not real. The Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit? The Patriarch said:
Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and tranquil. Such merit is not to be sought through worldly means.
The Emperor asked again, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Patriarch replied, "Vast emptiness—there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that faces me?
The Patriarch replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not attain realization.
The inscription reads: "One may place a single palm over it and gaze intently. Yao Fengqian wrote: "Within the clouds, the imperial city with its twin phoenix towers;
amidst the rain, ten thousand households among the spring trees."
The twenty-ninth patriarch, Grand Master Huìkě, was a native of Wúláo. He was the son of the Jī clan; his father’s name was Jí.

Having long prayed for offspring without success, one night a wondrous light illuminated the room, and his mother subsequently conceived. Thus, he was named Guāng at birth. From his youth, he was transcendent;
he read extensively through the archives of learning and was particularly skilled in discussing the *Lǎozi* and *Zhuāngzi*. Later, upon examining the Buddha-vehicle, he...
He cast everything away and left the household life under the Chan Master Baojing. He studied the doctrines of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna extensively.

At the age of thirty-three, he returned to Mount Xiangshan, where he sat in meditation throughout the day. After another eight years, while in a state of profound silence, he suddenly beheld a divine being who said to him, "You are about to receive the fruit [of enlightenment];
you must go south. The following day, he felt a pain in his head as if it were being pierced with needles. As he was about to seek medical treatment, suddenly—
A voice was heard from the air, saying, "This is a transformation of the bones. He went to see Huijing and recounted the matter.
Jing examined him and saw that his cranial bone (*uṣṇīṣa*) rose prominently, like five peaks emerging in splendor. Because of this divine anomaly, he changed his name to Shen Guang (Divine Light).
Jing said to the Patriarch, "Your marks are auspicious; yet the spirits have directed you toward the South. There, at Shaolin, is the Great Being Bodhidharma; he will surely be your teacher."

The Patriarch then proceeded to Shaoshi Mountain to attend upon Bodhidharma. There, Bodhidharma sat upright facing a wall; no instructions or exhortations were heard. The Patriarch reflected to himself:

"In the past, those who sought the Way would break their bones to extract marrow, pierce their flesh to provide sustenance for the hungry, spread their hair to cover the mud, and cast themselves from cliffs to feed tigers.
If the ancients were such as this, what person am I? Yet here I am. During a great snowfall, the Patriarch stood in attendance throughout the night until dawn, when the snow had accumulated.
He stood with his knees buried in the snow, bowing even more reverently. Bodhidharma looked at him and took pity on him, asking, "You have been standing in the snow for a long time; what do you seek?
The Patriarch wept sorrowfully and said, "I only pray that the Master will, out of compassion, open the gate of ambrosia and extensively deliver all sentient beings."

Bodhidharma said, "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of all Buddhas was attained through diligent effort over vast eons; one must be able to perform what is difficult to do and endure what is difficult to endure.
How can you hope for the True Vehicle with meager virtue and meager wisdom, with a frivolous mind and a haughty mind? Your toil and hardship will be in vain.
Hearing these exhortations, the Patriarch secretly took a sharp blade, severed his own left arm, and placed it before Bodhidharma. Bodhidharma knew this was the Dharma.
Huike then cut off his arm before Bodhidharma and said, "The Buddhas of all ages first sought the Way, forgetting their very forms for the sake of the Dharma.
Now that you have severed your arm before me, your request may indeed be granted. Thereupon, Bodhidharma changed his name to Huike. Huike then asked, "May I hear the Dharma-seal of the Buddhas?
Bodhidharma replied, "The Dharma-seal of the Buddhas is not obtained from another. Huike said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg [for its pacification]."

The Master [Huike] and Ananda were present. Bodhidharma said, "Bring forth your mind; I shall pacify it for you. After a long while, the Patriarch said, "I have searched for the mind, but it is utterly unattainable.
Bodhidharma said, "I have finished pacifying your mind for you. Nine years later, Bodhidharma wished to return to India.
The Master addressed his disciples, saying, "The time has come. You should each speak of what you have attained.

Dao Fu replied, "As I see it, one does not cling to words and letters, yet one does not depart from words and letters; this constitutes the functioning of the Way. Bodhidharma said, "You have obtained my skin.
Ni Zongchi said, "My current understanding is like that of Ānanda seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha. [Bodhidharma said,] "One."
"Having seen me, you shall not see me again. Bodhidharma said, "You have obtained my flesh. Daoyu replied, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates do not exist.
In my place of seeing, there is not a single dharma to be obtained. Bodhidharma said, "You have obtained my bone.
Finally, the Patriarch prostrated three times and stood in his place. Bodhidharma said, "You have obtained my marrow," and then he turned toward the Patriarch.
He said: "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to the Great Being Kāśyapa; it was passed down through successive entrustments until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you; you must protect and uphold it. I also bestow upon you this kashaya robe as a token of the Dharma.

Each has its own symbolic significance, which you should understand. The Patriarch said: "I pray that the Master will explain them. Bodhidharma replied: "Internally, there is the transmission of the Dharma Seal."

To certify the mind through realization, he externally entrusted him with the *kāṣāya* robe to establish the fundamental tenets. Yet, in later generations when the world grew corrupt, doubts vied to arise:
"He is a man from the Western Heaven; you are a son of this land. On what basis did you receive the Dharma? By what do you certify it?"
"You shall now receive this robe-transmission rite. Hereafter, when conditions become difficult, simply produce this robe along with my Dharma verses to manifest [the truth];

thus your transformation will be unimpeded. When two hundred years have passed since my parinirvāṇa, the robe will cease to be transmitted. The Dharma will pervade the entire realm of saṃsāra: those who clarify the Way will be many, but those who practice the Way will be few;
those who expound the principles will be many, but those who penetrate the principles will be few. They will secretly accord and subtly harmonize..."

Those who have realized this number in the millions; you should propagate it. Do not disparage those who have not yet awakened. With a single thought, if one turns the faculty of the mind, one is identical to original attainment.
Listen to my verse: "I originally came to this land to transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings. One flower opens into five petals."
"The result is spontaneously accomplished. Bodhidharma further said, "I have four fascicles of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, which I also entrust to you.
This is the essential gateway to the Tathāgata’s mind-ground, intended to cause all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter it. Since I arrived here,"
I have been poisoned five times in total. I once came forth myself to test it by placing a stone upon it; the stone split asunder.
This was because I originally departed from South India to come here to this Eastern Land, where I beheld that the Great State of China possessed the majestic air of the Mahāyāna.

Consequently, I crossed seas and deserts to seek the Dharma and its seekers. Our fates had not yet met, so I remained as if foolish and mute. Now that I have received your transmission, my purpose is fulfilled.
After [the previous patriarch] had passed away, the Patriarch went to the capital of Ye to guide and transform the fourfold assembly.
For thirty-four years, he then concealed his brilliance and blended with the common crowd, altering his appearance and demeanor. At times he entered wine shops; at times he passed by butcher stalls;

at times he engaged in street chatter; at times he followed common laborers. If someone asked him, "Master, you are a man of the Way; why do you act like this? the Patriarch replied, "I am simply training my own mind."
"What business is that of yours?
Baotai replied. "A withered stump ghost. Qian of Yao said, "There is no path for it to travel.
The thirty-second patriarch, Master Sengcan, was a man of unknown origin. In the second year of the Tianping era of the Northern Qi dynasty, at the age of...

When he was over forty years old, he went to visit Master Ke in his lay clothes and said, "Disciple, my body is afflicted by a wind ailment; I pray that you, O Upādhyāya, will perform the repentance for my transgressions.
Master Ke said, "Bring forth your transgressions, and I shall repent them for you. After a long while, the Patriarch said, "I have searched for my transgressions, but they are utterly unobtainable.
Master Ke said, "I have finished repenting your transgressions for you. You should dwell in accordance with the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. The Patriarch said, "Now..."
Upon seeing the Master, he already knew him to be a monk, yet he did not know what was meant by "Buddha-dharma.
The Great Master said, "This mind is the Buddha; this mind is the Dharma. Dharma and Buddha are non-dual; so too is the Jewel of the Sangha.
The Patriarch said, "Only today do I understand that the nature of sin is neither within, nor without, nor in between. As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha-dharma: they are non-dual."
Master Ke deeply esteemed him and immediately shaved his hair, saying, "He is my treasure. He should be named Sengcan.
On the eighteenth day of the third month of that year, he received full ordination at Guangfu Temple. From then on, his illness gradually improved.
After serving him for two years, Master Ke entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma, speaking this verse: "The ground of conditions exists from the beginning; By cause..."
"A flower grows from the element of earth, yet originally there was no seed; the flower, moreover, has never been born. He further said, "You have received my instruction;
you should dwell in the deep mountains and must not yet go forth to transform others. There will be national calamity. This is what Prajñātāra predicted in advance:
that which is called "though auspicious within the mind, it is ominous without" refers to this. I, too, have karmic debts from past lives, which I shall now repay. You—

Reflect deeply upon the Sage’s prediction; do not encounter the hardships of the world. Proceed with skillful departure and skillful conduct, awaiting the time to transmit [the Dharma] to the Patriarch.

The Patriarch [Huineng] composed the *Inscription on Faith*: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing. Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and you will be transparently clear and bright.

A difference of a hair's breadth results in a gap as vast as heaven and earth. If you wish for it to manifest before you, do not maintain notions of favorability or opposition. When favorability and opposition contend with one another, this..."

This is a sickness of the mind. Failing to recognize the profound essence, one merely exerts oneself in the pursuit of stillness. When [the mind] is perfectly identical to the great void, there is neither deficiency nor excess.

It is precisely because of grasping and rejecting that one falls short. Do not pursue conditioned objects; do not dwell in the patience of emptiness. With a single state of equanimity, all things vanish of themselves.
To stop movement by returning to stillness—stopping further intensifies the movement. Merely lingering on two sides, how can one know the One? One.
The various categories do not interpenetrate; in both cases, one’s effort is lost. To dispatch existence by means of non-existence is to turn one's back on emptiness from within emptiness.

Excessive words and excessive deliberation lead further away from accord. When speech is cut off and deliberation ceases, there is nowhere that does not penetrate. Returning to the root, one attains the essential meaning; following illumination, one loses the source.
A moment of returning-illumination surpasses the previous emptiness. That the previous emptiness underwent transformation was entirely due to deluded vision. Do not seek the truth; simply...
One must cease the two views and not dwell in them; be careful not to pursue them. As soon as there is right and wrong, one becomes distracted and loses the mind.

Because duality arises from unity, do not even cling to that unity. When the one mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. With no fault, there are no dharmas; with no arising, there is no mind.
The capacity [of the mind] ceases through objects, and objects sink along with the capacity. Objects exist because of the capacity, and the capacity exists because of objects. Thus it is with desire.

Know that these two segments originally constitute a single emptiness. This single emptiness is identical to the two; together they encompass the myriad phenomena. When one does not perceive the distinction between the refined and the coarse, how could there be partiality?

The substance of the Great Way is vast; it is neither easy nor difficult. Those with narrow views harbor doubts; the more hurried they are, the slower they progress. To cling to it is to lose the proper measure and inevitably enter a deviant path.
To let go naturally, its substance has no coming or staying. To follow one's nature is to accord with the Way; thus one wanders in ease.

To distance oneself from afflictions is to sever them; to fix one's mindfulness while deviating from the Truth is to fall into the darkness of torpor. Torpor is unwholesome, and being unwholesome, it exhausts the spirit. What use is there for distinguishing between the distant and the intimate?
If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not loathe the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). If you do not loathe the six sense-objects, you will be identical to Perfect Enlightenment.

The wise act without artifice (*anabhisaṃskāra*); the foolish bind themselves. There is no dharma other than the Dharma, yet they deludedly become attached to it. To employ the mind by means of the mind—is this not a great error? Delusion!

Birth brings stillness and turmoil; awakening reveals that there is neither good nor evil. All dualistic extremes arise from one’s own deliberations. They are like dreams, illusions, or flowers in the sky—why labor to grasp them?
Let gain and loss, right and wrong, be cast off all at once. If the eye does not sleep, all dreams vanish of their own accord; if the mind does not diverge, the myriad dharmas are as one.
When this oneness embodies the profound mystery, one sits motionless, forgetting all conditions. Viewing the myriad dharmas as equal, one returns to the source.
Furthermore, it is spontaneous. It dissolves that which constitutes it; it cannot be compared or likened. Stillness and movement are without movement;

movement and stillness are without stillness. Since both are not established, how could there be a "one"? Reaching the ultimate limit, no rules or patterns remain. The mind accords with equality, and all conditioned activities cease.
Doubt is completely purified, and right faith becomes straightened and upright. Nothing remains; there is nothing to be remembered. It is empty.
Luminosity illuminates itself; it does not labor with mind or power. It is not a realm of discursive thought, difficult for the intellect and emotions to fathom.

The *tathatā* dharma-realm has neither other nor self. One must urgently seek resonance with it; speak only of non-duality. Where there is no duality, all are identical; there is nothing that is not encompassed.
The wise of the ten directions all enter this school. This school is neither extended nor abbreviated: in a single thought-moment is ten thousand years. It is neither here nor not here. Ten...
Right before one’s eyes, the extremely small is identical to the great; forgetting all boundaries, the extremely great is identical to the small.
Existence is non-existence, and non-existence is existence. If it were not thus, there would be no need to maintain [this state]. One is all, and all is one.
If you can simply act in this way, why worry that anything will not be accomplished? Faith is non-dual, and non-duality is faith. Thus it is said.
The path of speech is severed; it belongs neither to the past, the future, nor the present.

The thirty-first patriarch, Grand Master Daoxin, was surnamed Sima. His family had resided for generations in Henei, later migrating to Guangji County in Qizhou.
From birth he was exceptionally gifted; from childhood he admired the school of emptiness, and his mastery of the various gates of liberation appeared as if it were the result of past habituation.
At the age of fourteen, he went to pay homage to Grand Master Sengcan, saying: "I pray that the Upādhyāya will, out of compassion, grant me liberation."
Dafu asked, "Who has bound you? The Patriarch said, "No one has bound me. Dafu said, "If that is so, why do you seek liberation?

At these words, the Patriarch attained great enlightenment. He served Dafu with diligence for nine years. Later, he received full ordination in Jizhou and continued to serve his master with even greater reverence.

Dafu repeatedly tested him on the profound and subtle mysteries; knowing that his karmic conditions were ripe, he entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma. The verse said: "Though the seeds of the flower..."
Regarding the "ground": flowers grow from the seeds of the earth; if no one sows the seeds, the flowers will cease to grow entirely upon that ground. It is further said:
"In the past, after the Great Master Ka received my Dharma, he went to the capital of Ye to propagate the teachings for over thirty years. Now that I have found you."
"Why linger here? he asked, and immediately departed for Mount Luofu. Having inherited the legacy of the Patriarch, the Master restrained his mind and did not sleep;
for sixty years, his side never touched his mat. In the thirteenth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he led his disciples to Jizhou.

There they encountered a band of rebels surrounding the city, which remained besieged for seventy days without resolution. The multitude was terrified, and the Patriarch took pity on them, instructing them to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.

At that time, when a band of rebels looked toward the battlements and saw no divine soldiers, they said to one another, "There must be extraordinary people within the city," and they gradually withdrew.
In the year of Guimao during the Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong, drawn to the flavor of the Master’s Way and wishing to behold his dignified bearing, issued an edict for him to come to the capital.
Master Zu submitted a memorial declining the invitation three times in succession. On the fourth occasion, the Emperor sent an envoy with these words:
"If he does not rise, bring his head here. The messenger was sent to the mountain to deliver this decree. Sengzu then extended his neck toward the blade; his countenance remained solemn and composed.
When the messenger returned and reported these circumstances to the Emperor, the Emperor’s respect and admiration for him grew even greater.

The thirty-second patriarch, Master Hongren, was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou.

In the Jia-shen year of the Tang dynasty’s Wude era, Daoxin returned to Qichun and resided at Mount Pòtóu. Disciples gathered like clouds. One day, while traveling to Huangmei County, he encountered Huineng on the road.

Their family was extremely poor; from childhood, he gathered firewood and sold it to support his mother. One day, while carrying firewood through the marketplace, he passed by.

He asked the guest, "What dharma is this? The guest replied, "This is the *Vajracchedikā*. The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Huineng of East Mountain at Huangmei, constantly teaches people to recite this sūtra.

A certain guest was preparing a year’s provisions for his mother and, taking his leave, traveled directly to Shaoyang Prefecture.

she had been reading the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and when the Patriarch briefly listened to her, he immediately explained its meaning for her. The nun then took up the scroll and asked about the characters, to which the Patriarch replied:

The Patriarch replied, "The wondrous principle of the Buddhas has nothing to do with written words. The nun was struck with wonder and amazement; she informed the elders of her village and invited him to reside at Baolin Monastery.

Although the monastery had been in ruins for a long time, the fourfold assembly labored to restore it, gathering there morning and night until it was suddenly transformed into a magnificent monastic complex. The Patriarch then said:
"I seek the Great Dharma; what is the purpose of staying here? he said, and so he abandoned it. He traveled to Huangmei and attended upon Master Hongren.
Hongren asked, "Where have you come from? The Patriarch replied, "From Lingnan. Hongren asked, "What do you wish to seek? The Patriarch replied, "I seek only to become a Buddha.
Hongren said, "People of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature; how can you become a Buddha? The Patriarch replied, "People certainly have [Buddha-nature], regardless of north or south."
Huineng said, "The Buddha-nature is not like that. Why should you force me to perform manual labor? Faren said, "My disciple’s own mind constantly gives rise to wisdom;
never departing from its own nature, it is itself a field of merit. I do not know what task the Master would have me perform.
Faren said, "This barbarian has a very sharp root-nature. Go to the fodder shed! Huineng prostrated at his feet and withdrew, then entered the rice-hulling workshop and began his service.
He labored with the pestle and mortar, day and night without ceasing, for eight months. Knowing that the time for the transmission had arrived, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"The True Dharma is difficult to understand; it must not be merely memorized. Let my words be your own responsibility; you all may now go as you please."

He recited a verse. If his words and meaning were in perfect accord with the Master’s intent, then both the robe and the Dharma would be transmitted to him. At that time, there were over seven hundred monks in the assembly.
Among them was the senior monk (Upādhyāya) Shenxiu, whose learning encompassed both Buddhist and secular classics, and whom the multitude revered and looked up to.

They all commended him, saying, "Were it not for the venerable Shenxiu, who else would dare to receive this? Having secretly heard the acclaim of the assembly, Shenxiu no longer reflected further; he then wrote [the verse] upon the wall of the corridor.
A verse says: "The body is the Bodhi tree; / The mind is like a bright mirror stand. / At all times diligently wipe it clean, / And let no dust or grime settle upon it.
While walking about for meditation, Huineng suddenly saw this verse and recognized it as the work of Shenxiu. He then praised it, saying:
"If future generations rely on this to practice, they too shall attain the supreme fruit. Originally, he had intended to have the scholar Lu Zhen [copy the verse] upon the wall.
He was about to paint a transformation scene of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, but upon seeing the verses inscribed on the wall, he stopped painting and instead instructed everyone to recite them.
While Huineng was at the rice-grinding shed, he suddenly heard someone reciting the verses and asked his fellow practitioners, "What chapter or passage is this?

His companions replied, "You do not know that the Master has requested dharma-heirs and ordered each of you to compose a verse expressing your mind. This is the one composed by Venerable Xiu; the Master..."
[The Master] praised him deeply, saying, "He will surely be entrusted with the Dharma and the robe. The Patriarch asked, "What was his verse? His fellow student recited it for him.
After a long silence, the Patriarch said, "It is beautiful, yet it is not yet fully realized. The fellow student rebuked him, saying, "How could an ordinary person like me know this?
Do not utter such delirious words. The Patriarch replied, "Do you not believe me? I wish to join you with a verse of my own. The fellow student did not [consent].
He replied, "We looked at each other and laughed. That night, the Patriarch secretly informed a young boy and led him to the corridor.
Holding a candle himself, the Patriarch requested the Vice-Governor Zhang Ruyong to write a verse beside that of Xu You, saying:
"Bodhi originally has no tree; The bright mirror is likewise not a stand. Fundamentally there is not a single thing— Where could dust and grime settle? Later, when [Xu] Ren saw this, he was moved.
The verse says: "Who made this? Its nature has not yet been seen. Hearing these words, Huineng paid them no further mind.

That night, Huineng went secretly to the rice-hulling room and asked, "Is the rice white yet? The Sixth Patriarch replied, "It is white, but it has not yet been sifted. Huineng struck the pestle three times with his staff;

the Patriarch immediately beat the drum three times and entered his room. Huineng again questioned him regarding his initial awakening, to which [the Patriarch] responded that there was nothing to be attained.

As he dwelt there, he gave rise to this thought: "Under the words of the Patriarch, I have attained great enlightenment. I have realized that all phenomena do not depart from self-nature (*svabhāva*).
How unexpected it is that self-nature is fundamentally pure! How unexpected it is that self-nature is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing!
How unexpected it is that self-nature is fundamentally complete! How unexpected it is that self-nature is fundamentally unmoving! How unexpected it is that self-nature can..."

He gave rise to the myriad dharmas. Through patient endurance and knowledge, he awakened to his original nature. He said to the Patriarch, "If one does not recognize the original nature, studying the Dharma is of no benefit.
If one recognizes the fundamental mind and perceives one's own original nature, one is then called a Great Man, a Teacher of Gods and Humans, and a Buddha.

He further declared, "The appearance of all Buddhas in the world is for the sake of this one great matter. Therefore, they guide beings according to their capacities, whether great or small; thus there are the ten stages (bhūmis) and the three [vehicles]."

Taking the principles of the sudden and gradual vehicles as the gateway of the teaching, he entrusted the unsurpassed, subtle, secret, perfectly luminous, and true *Dharmaparyāya*—the Treasury of the True Eye of the Dharma—to the preeminent Venerable Mahākāśyapa.

It was transmitted in succession through twenty-eight generations until it reached Bodhidharma, who arrived in this land. There he met the Great Master Huike, from whom it has been inherited down to the present day. By means of this Dharma...

As for those who receive the robe, their lives are as precarious as a strand of silk hanging from a beam. The Patriarch asked, "Where should I go into seclusion? Huineng replied, "Whenever you encounter the state of *huai* (contentment/serenity), then [go]."

After the Patriarch had paid his respects and taken his leave, he traveled south for two months until he reached Mount Dayu. There, the monk Huiming—formerly a general—arrived with several hundred men, intending to seize his robe and bowl.

can it be won by force? Hui Ming tried to lift the robe and bowl but could not move them. He then said, "I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of the robe.

Under these words, Huiming attained great enlightenment. He asked again, "Beyond these secret words and secret meanings, is there still another secret intent?
The Patriarch said, "That which I have spoken to you is not secret. If you turn back and reflect, the secret is right here."

The Patriarch said, "If it is so, then I and you shall share the same teacher at Huangmei. Guard and uphold [the Dharma] well. Huiming asked again, "What of Huiming now?"
"Where have you gone? The Patriarch replied, "When I meet Yuan, I shall stop; when I encounter Meng, I shall dwell.

Regarding the Dharma, there was none superior to him among gods or men. Meeting with his fellow student Tanyan, they went together to visit Hui'an of Mount Song.

In the second year of the Xiāntián era, he went to Mount Heng and resided at Bānrúo Monastery. Addressing the assembly, he said: "All phenomena arise from the mind;
the mind has no place of origin, and phenomena have no place to abide. If one penetrates the ground of the mind, all actions will be unimpeded.

The Master said, "When you, Venerable Sir, had not yet left the household life, where did your physical form go? The monk said, "Now that you have become [a monk], why do you not reflect [on this]?

He first resided at Mount Fojie in Jianyang, then moved to Linchuan, and subsequently went to Gonggong Mountain in Nankang. A monk asked: "Leaving behind..."
The four propositions are cut off and the hundred negations exhausted. "I pray you, Master, point directly to the meaning of the coming from the West. The Master said, "I am weary today;

The thirty-sixth patriarch, Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai, was born into the Wang family of Changle in Fuzhou. In his childhood...

Accompanying his mother to a temple, he pointed to a Buddha image and asked her, "Who is this? His mother replied, "It is the Buddha. The Master said, "His form and appearance are no different from those of humans;
I too shall become a Buddha in the future. At the age of seven, he left the secular world. He thoroughly mastered the three studies and attended Mazu as his attendant.
Whenever a donor brought offerings of rice for the midday meal, as soon as the Master lifted the lid of the tray, Mazu would [suddenly strike him].
Holding up a piece of fried cake, he asked, "What is this? He continued in this manner for three years.
One day, while attending upon Mazu, they were walking along when they saw a flock of wild ducks fly past. Mazu asked, "What is that? The Master replied, "Wild ducks."
Mazu asked, "Where have you gone? The Master replied, "I flew away. Mazu then seized the Master by the nose and twisted it;
the Master cried out in pain. Mazu said, "And yet you say you flew away? At these words, the Master attained realization.
He returned to the attendants' quarters and wept bitterly. A colleague asked him, "Are you thinking of your parents? The Master replied, "No."

[The attendant] asked, "Was he cursed by someone? The Master said, "No. [The attendant] asked, "Then why is he crying? The Master said, "My nostrils were pinched by the Great Master; it hurts me to the core.
A fellow practitioner asked, "What circumstance was there that did not accord with him? The Master said, "You should ask the Abbot about it.
The fellow practitioner then asked Mazu, "What circumstance did Attendant Hai have that did not accord with him? He is currently in his quarters."
While weeping, he informed the Abbot, who said, "The Master has explained it for you. Mazu replied, "It is he who understands; you should ask him yourself.
When they returned to the quarters together, the Abbot said, "The Master said, 'You understand,' and told me to ask you myself.
The Master then laughed heartily. His companion asked, "Just now you were weeping; why are you laughing now? The Master said, "Just now I was weeping."
He laughed now, leaving his colleagues bewildered. The next day, when Mazu ascended the seat and the assembly had just gathered, the Master stepped forward and rolled up the cushion.
Mazu immediately descended from the seat. The Master followed him to the abbot’s quarters, where Mazu said, "I have not yet spoken a word."
"You have been very convenient; now roll up your mat. The Master said, "Yesterday I was pinched by you, O Monk, and my nose still aches.
Mazu asked, "Where did you direct your attention yesterday? The Master replied, "At my nose. Mazu said, "Today it does not ache anymore."
Mazu said, "You have deeply understood yesterday's matter. The Master bowed and withdrew.

Mazu said, "Is this its function? Or is it apart from its function? The Master hung the whisk back in its original place. Mazu let out a thunderous shout, which left the Master deaf in both ears for three days.

The thirty-seventh patriarch, Chan Master Huangbo Xiyun, was a native of Min. In his youth, he left the household life at Mount Huangbo in his home prefecture.
A protuberance on his forehead rose like a pearl; his speech was clear and resonant, and his disposition was profound and serene.

Later, while traveling to Tiantai, he encountered a monk with whom he conversed and laughed as if they were old acquaintances. Upon looking closely, [the master] saw that the other’s gaze pierced people. Thereupon—

The Master said, "If you wish to cross, brother, cross by yourself. The monk immediately lifted his robes and stepped into the waves as if treading on level ground.
Looking back, he called out, "Come across! Come across! The Master said, "Tsk! You self-satisfied fellow; had I known this earlier, I would have cut off your shins. The monk sighed in admiration.

He said, "A true vessel for the Mahāyāna Dharma; I am not his equal. Having finished speaking, he vanished. Upon arriving in the capital of Luoyang, he went about begging, the sound of his bowl being filled echoing as he chanted.

The master from Suofa took his leave shortly thereafter. The old woman told him, "You should go to Nanchang to see Master Ma.
Upon arriving in Nanchang, Master Ma had already passed away. He then proceeded to Shimen. While he was paying respects at the stupa, Master Baizhang was dwelling nearby in a grass hut.
He went to visit Baizhang, who asked, "Majestic and dignified as you are, from where have you come? The master replied:

After a long silence, the Teacher said, "One must not allow the lineage to be severed for future generations. The Master said, "I had thought you were..."

Dongshan said, "So it is, so it is. When the student's vision equals that of the teacher, the teacher’s virtue is reduced by half."
"One whose insight surpasses that of the teacher is alone worthy of receiving the transmission. You possess a vision that greatly exceeds your teacher’s. The Master then bowed.

Now, however, you say, "Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much. What principle have you seen? Speak quickly! Speak quickly!
The Master struck Daoyu three times in the ribs. Daoyu pushed him away and said, "Your teacher is Huangbo; it is none of my business.
The Master took his leave of Daoyu and returned to Huangbo. Upon seeing him, Huangbo asked, "This fellow has been coming and going..."
[The Master] said, "I am going. When will there ever be an end to this? The Teacher said, "It is precisely because my old wife’s heart is so earnest that I have come to pay my respects.
He then stood in attendance. Huangbo asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "Yesterday, I received the Compassionate Command of the Abbot and was sent to visit Dayu;

Huangbo said, "This madman has come here to pull at the tiger's whiskers. The Master then shouted. Huangbo called to an attendant and said, "Take this madman away to attend to the hall duties.
Later, while the Master was planting pine trees, Huangbo said, "Why are you planting so many pines in the deep mountains?"
"What are you doing? the Master asked. The teacher replied, "First, to provide a model for the mountain gate; second, to serve as a banner for future generations.
Having said this, he struck the ground three times with his mattock. Huangbo said, "Even so, you have already received thirty blows from me.
The teacher struck the ground three times again and let out a long sigh. Huangbo said, "My lineage has reached you; it will flourish greatly."
At that time, there were five hundred monks at Jingshan, yet few came to seek instruction from Huangbo.
He sent the Master to Jingshan and said to him, "When you arrive there, what will you do? The Master replied, "Once I have arrived there, I shall naturally have my own expedient means.

When the Master reached Jingshan, he went straight up to the Dharma Hall with his travel pack on his back. Upon seeing Jingshan, as the latter was just raising his head, the Master let out a shout. Jingshan—
Mount Jing was about to open his mouth when the Master shook his sleeves and departed. Shortly thereafter, a monk asked, "What were the words and phrases of this monk from Mount Jing just now?
[The monk] then shouted at the Master. Mount Jing said, "This monk comes from Huangbo’s assembly. Do you wish to know? Go ask him yourself.

The Master traveled several li, then felt doubt about this matter and returned to stay for the remainder of the summer. Later, he took his leave of Baizhang again. Baizhang asked, "Where are you going?

The Master replied, "Not south of the Yellow River; I am going straight back north of it. Baizhang struck him again. The Master grabbed him and gave him a slap. Baizhang laughed heartily and then called out:
The attendant brought Master Baizhang’s former meditation board and desk. The Master said, "Attendant, bring fire. Huangbo said, "Not so. You simply take it away;
in the future, you shall cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven. The Master then dispatched a letter for Huangbo.
When he arrived at Mount Gui, Yangshan was serving as the guest prefect. Upon receiving the letter, Yangshan immediately asked, "This one..."
"This is Huangbo's [staff]. "Which one is the messenger's? The Master then struck him. Yangshan held him back, saying, "Elder brother, you know this sort of business;
let it be. Together they went to see Guishan. Guishan asked, "Elder brother Huangbo, how many followers do you have?
The Master said, "Seven hundred. Guishan said, "Who acts as their leader? The Master said, "Just now..."
Having finished reading the letter, the Master asked, "How many followers does the Venerable Huishan have here?
Huishan replied, "One thousand five hundred. The Master said, "That is too many. Huishan said, "The elder brother Huangbo has no fewer than that either."
When the Master took his leave of Guishan, Yangshan saw him out and said, "In the future you shall go north; there will be a place for you to dwell.
The Master said, "How could such a thing be? Yangshan said, "Once you have gone, there will be someone to assist you, my elder brother."
"This man has only a head but no tail; he has a beginning but no end. Later, when the Master was residing at Linji in Zhenzhou, his disciples gathered like clouds.
One day, the Master said to the two senior monks, Puhua and Kefu, "I wish to establish the school of Huangbo here.
You two should challenge me. The two men respectfully withdrew. Three days later, Puhua...
Huaqie came up and asked, "What did you say three days ago, Master? The Master struck him.
Three days later, Kefu came up and asked, "Why did you strike Puhua three days ago, Master? The Master struck him as well. The Master once addressed the assembly, saying:
"When students from various quarters come here, I categorize them according to their three types of spiritual capacity. As he spoke, he drew a circle.
If one of middling or inferior faculties comes, I then take away their object but do not remove their dharma.

If one of middling or superior faculties comes, I then take away both their object and their dharma. If one of the highest faculties comes, I then take away their object, their dharma, and their person.
If someone with extraordinary insight should come here, I, this mountain monk, will manifest my entire being in response, bypassing all levels of capacity.
When you, Great Virtue, arrive here, the place where students exert their efforts is not a path through which the wind can pass; even a spark of stone or a flash of lightning has already passed by.
If a student’s eyes waver for a moment, there is no connection; if the mind intends to act, it is already mistaken; if a thought stirs, it is already deviant.
There was one who understood it as being not apart from what is before one's eyes.
Baotiao said, "The stream in the West flows swiftly; even an ox-calf is worth looking at. Yao Feng Qian said, "Four eyes gaze upon one another."
The thirty-ninth patriarch, Chan Master Xinghua Cunjian, was originally the attendant to Linji.
When Luofu came to visit him, Linji asked, "Where have you come from? Luofu replied, "From Luancheng. Linji said, "May I ask you something?
Luofu said, "A newly ordained monk does not understand. Linji remarked, "If one were to raze the Great Tang Empire, could one find even a single person who does not understand?"
"Neither. Go to the hall. The Master followed him and asked, "Just now, regarding that newly arrived monk, did you strip him of his status or not?
Nanquan said, "Who am I to concern myself with whether he was stripped or not? The Master said, "The Master only knows how to..."
He took the dying sparrow and tossed it to the ground, failing to cover it over with a turning word. Jie asked, "And what about you?
The Master said, "I ask the Abbot to act as the newcomer. Jie then said, "The new precept-holder does not understand.
The Master said, "Rather, this is my own fault. Jie said, "Your words conceal the peak. As the Master hesitated, Jie struck him. That evening, Jie...
He also said, "Today I asked him: 'The newly arrived one is like striking a dying sparrow on the ground, or hitting it right in its nest.

But as soon as you managed to produce a word, he shouted, 'Get up! and struck you, sending you into the blue clouds. The Master said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated. Jie then struck him.
Later, while serving as the head seat (chief priest) in the assembly of Sansheng, he would often say, "I traveled southward."
His feet had never once been touched by the tip of a staff. A man who understood the Buddha-dharma heard of this;
Sansheng asked him, "What kind of eye do you possess that you speak in such a manner? The Master then gave a shout. Sansheng said, "It must be you who can do so.
Later, when Da’jue heard this account being cited, he remarked, "How could the wind ever blow all the way to Da’jue’s gate?"
[The Master] returned. Later, he arrived at Da’jue and served as the head of the monastery (*yuanzhu*).
One day, Da’jue called out to him, “I have heard you say that during your journey southward, you have never once struck upon a single person who understands the Buddha-dharma.
On what basis do you speak in such a manner? The Master then gave a shout. Da’jue struck him. The Master shouted again. Da’jue—
He struck him again. The next day, as the Master was passing by the Dharma Hall, Yuanjue summoned the head of the monastery and said, "I have a doubt regarding those two shouts you gave yesterday.
