In the second year of the Qianyou era of the illegitimate Han dynasty, as the governor had transferred his administration to Yingzhou, the Master again fled from bandits and went to rely upon him.
The governor hosted him in the prefectural study hall. Once the rebellion was quelled, there was a man named Song Tai in Ruzhou.
The Master established a monastery for him as a precious vihāra, naming it Xinsi (New Temple), and invited the Master to reside there.
His Dharma seat was preeminent throughout the world, and students came from afar. Ascending the seat, he said: "The former Master said: 'If you wish to attain intimacy, do not bring questions.
Do you understand? The question is in the place of the answer; the answer is in the place of the question. Although this is so, sometimes the question is not in the answer."
The answer lies not where the question lies. If you hesitate to deliberate, this old monk is already beneath your heels.
Generally speaking, the eyes of one who studies the Way must be ready to act when the occasion arises; let the great function manifest before you, and do not confine yourself to minor details.

Even if you gain realization before a word is spoken, you still remain stuck in the shell of delusion; even if you master the meaning beneath a phrase, you cannot avoid wild views wherever you encounter the path. You should...
Hitherto, you have relied on others to form interpretations, resulting in two divergent paths—clarity and obscurity.

I shall now sweep all these away for you, so that each and every one of you may, like a lion cub, let out a "ta-ya" cry before the assembly as a testament to your realization; with a single roar, you shall stand firm and solitary like a cliff rising ten thousand fathoms high.

"Who would dare look at this with a direct eye? To look is to blind one's own eyes. The Master said: "If you establish even a single speck of dust, the state and its family will flourish, but the village elders will frown.
If you do not establish even a single speck of dust, the state and its family will perish, but the village elders will be at peace."
Regarding this clarity, the master has no share; it is entirely the old monk. Regarding this lack of clarity, the old monk is precisely the master.
Both the master and the old monk can cause all people in the world to awaken, and both can cause all people in the world to go blind.
Do you wish to recognize the master? [He] pats his left knee and says: "This here is [the master]. Do you wish to recognize the old monk? [He] pats [his right knee].
The Right Knee said: "At that moment, was there no one who could master the pivot? Baotai said:
"Without relying on remembering a single word, without employing a single effort, without blinking an eye, and without even exhaling a breath.
Yaofeng Qian said: "Let the ducks listen to the thunder."
The forty-second patriarch, Chan Master Shoushan Shengnian, was born into the Di clan in Lai Prefecture.

In his youth, he left home and received ordination at Nan Chan Temple. He was a man of simple gravity and refined discernment, who devoted himself exclusively to the practice of dhūta and the recitation of the Lotus Sūtra.
The monastic communities revered him, and they called him "Nian Fahua" (Lotus-Chanting Nian). Later, he joined the assembly at Fengxue.
Chong served as the guest prefect. One day, while standing in attendance, Xue shed tears and told him, "It is my misfortune that the Way of Linji is on the verge of collapsing upon reaching me.
The Master said, "Looking at this assembly, is there not anyone [worthy]? Xue replied:
"The clever are many; those who have seen their nature are few. The Master asked, "What about someone like me?

Xue said, "Although I have long looked forward to you, I still fear that you may remain attached to this scripture and be unable to let it go. The Master said, "This is also a matter of concern; I wish to hear its essential point.
Xue then ascended the hall and raised the following: "The World-Honored One turned his blue-lotus eyes toward the great assembly and said: [He then quoted the scripture].
"At this very moment, tell me: what is being said? If you say it is 'speaking without speaking,' that would be to bury the former sages.
So tell me, what is being said? The Master then shook his sleeves and went down; Xue threw down his staff and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
A attendant followed him and requested further instruction, saying, "Why did Nian Fahua not respond to the Master?"
Xue said, "I am thinking of the assembly at the Lotus Sutra. The following day, the Master and Zhen the Head Gardener went together to pay their respects.
Xue asked Zhen, "How is it that the World-Honored One speaks what is not spoken? Zhen replied, "The magpie cries atop the tree.
Xue said, "You have accumulated so much foolish merit; why do you not investigate the meaning of these words? He then asked the Master, "As for you..."
"How is it? The Master said, "Moving one's countenance to reveal the ancient path; not falling into the silent mechanism.
Xue said to Zhen, "Why do you not look at the commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra*? On another day, Xue ascended the seat and looked out over the assembly;
the Master then descended. Xue immediately returned to his quarters. From this time on, his reputation was esteemed throughout all quarters. Shoushan was in the city of Ru.
The Master resided in a remote and desolate place, intending to remain there for the rest of his life. Those who entered his gate were all seasoned monks from the great monasteries (*conglin*);
the Master invariably subjected them to rigorous examination, and only about twenty or so remained.

Nevertheless, when people throughout the world spoke of the preeminent Dharma seats, they invariably pointed to Shoushan. He once composed a verse on the "Iron Lineage" (*gangzong*), which says: "Alas, you clumsy young man! (Fenyang)

The commentary says: "Naturally pure and distinct," yet no one recognizes his ingenuity. (Operating the mechanism without showing his face,) he breaks through the Fenglin Barrier. (Having swept away all cleverness,) he stands upon the water wearing boots.
(Dust and mud remain distinct from him. "Alas, you clever girl! (Fenyang said: "Wondrous wisdom is perfectly integrated. Though she throws the shuttle, she does not know how to weave.

(If there is no interval, merit cannot be established. Look at that cock-fighter: (observing from the sidelines the leaping and pecking, he strives for victory without injuring himself). Even the water buffalo does not know (that with its full strength it can bear the burden without showing its horns).
The inscription states: "There are cases and labels; there are divisions and volumes. By day they are bright by the windows; by night they rely on lamps and candles.
Yao’s domain lies hidden [within], while the soaring eaves and railings rub against the clouds and mist. Precious bells chime in harmony, and jeweled nets are interspersed."
The forty-third patriarch, Chan Master Shanzhao of Taizi Monastery in Fenzhou, was born into the Yu clan and was a native of Taiyuan.

His character and insight were profound and far-reaching; he was naturally refined from his youth and possessed great wisdom. Regarding all forms of written literature, he did not rely on the instruction of teachers.

He naturally attained profound understanding. At the age of fourteen, his parents passed away one after the other. In his solitary suffering and weary of the phenomena of the world, he shaved his hair, received full ordination, and set out on a pilgrimage with a staff.
Wherever he went, he stayed but briefly; he took no pleasure in sightseeing. When some criticized him for lacking aesthetic refinement, the Master sighed and said:
"How vulgar are such words! Since the time of our predecessors, those who first practiced *dhūta* (ascetic travel) did so precisely because their holy minds were not yet [at peace]."

"Penetration is merely the driving force of discernment; it does not depend on mountains or rivers. Throughout his travels to various regions, the Master encountered seventy-one veteran masters, from all of whom he perfectly grasped their respective lineages.
He was particularly fond of discussing the Cao-Dong school. Zen Master Shimen Che was a preeminent figure of that lineage.
The Master composed the "Five Ranks Verses" and showed them to him, saying: "The five ranks are to be sought through practice."
One must know this for certain: the slightest movement is already a deviation. Who can understand the Vajra piercing its case? Only Nanda has the foremost mechanism.
A single glance causes the three realms to fall silent; a shake of the bell causes the nine heavens to return to their place.

In the midst of the correct, the subtle grasp penetrates through mutual interplay. Should one hesitate, the sharp edge loses its majesty. [The Master] struck his palm and praised him as excellent. Thus did the Master conclude.
Suspecting that the descendants of Linji possessed some extraordinary quality, he finally went to Shoushan and asked, "What is the meaning of Baizhang’s statement regarding rolling up the bamboo mat?
Shoushan replied, "The dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, and the entire body is revealed. The Master asked, "What is your own meaning, Master?

Shoushan said, "Where the Elephant King walks, there are no traces of foxes. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment; rising from his prostration, he said, "Ten thousand ages, the azure pool is a realm of emptiness."
"Month after month, only after repeated searching can one finally come to know. A questioner asked, "What principle have you seen that you are so readily willing [to stay]?

The Master said, "This is precisely where I shall lay down my body and life. Having served him with great diligence for a long time, he took his leave and traveled between the regions of Xiang and Heng.
Zhang Gong Maozong, the Governor of Changsha, invited the Master to choose among four famous monasteries to reside in. The Master smiled and said, "One..."

In the evening, he withdrew and traveled north to the regions of Xiang and Mian, taking up residence at Baima Temple. When Governor Liu Gongchangyan heard of this, he went to pay his respects and lamented that he had met the Master so late.
At that time, the seats of Dongshan, Guyin, and Huichang were all vacant, and the community discussed inviting the Master to fill one of them.

The Governor requested that he choose among them, but the Master gestured dismissively with his hand and said, "I am but a long-wandering monk who sells rice gruel; my purpose is to transmit the Mind-essence of the Buddha. It was not [his intent].
This was a minor post. He declined eight successive invitations, remaining firm in his refusal and refusing to answer.

In the fourth year of the Chunhua era, after Shoushan had passed away, more than a thousand monastics and laypeople from the western regions united their efforts to draft a formal petition. They dispatched the śramaṇa Qichong to invite him to serve as the abbot of the Taizi Yuan at Fenzhou Taiping Temple.
The Master remained behind closed doors with his pillow high, but Qichong forced his way through the door and remonstrated with him, saying, "The Buddha..."

The Dharma is a matter of great importance; withdrawing into quietude is but a minor detail. Fengxue feared that he would fail to respond to the prophecy and worried that the fundamental tenets of our school would fall into ruin.

Fortunately, there was the former master; yet the former master has already passed away. You, who possess the strength to shoulder the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata—how can you wish to sleep peacefully at such a time?
The Master started up in alarm and, grasping Cōng’s hand, said, "If it were not for you, I would never have heard these words. He then hurriedly prepared [the necessary provisions].
Yanwu said, "I am going. Upon his arrival, he sat in meditation upon a single mat for thirty years, his feet never crossing the threshold.

Monastics and laypeople throughout the world admired and revered him, yet dared not call him by name; they all simply referred to him as "The Master of Fenzhou. Since the region of Bingzhou and Fenzhou was bitterly cold, the Master discontinued the evening assemblies.
A certain bhikṣu arrived, shaking his mendicant’s staff, and said to the Master, “There are six great beings (mahāsattvas) in the assembly;

why do you not preach the Dharma? Having finished speaking, he ascended into the air and departed. The Master secretly recorded this in a verse, saying: “The foreign monk’s golden staff radiates light.”
Having requested the Dharma at Fenyang, six men became great vessels. I urge you to propagate it. At that time, Chuyuan and Shouzhi were the preeminent leaders.
Entering the hall, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Now, one who expounds the Dharma must possess the Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality.

If one does not possess the Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality, they cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, nor differentiate between the monastic and the lay; they will be unable to act as a guide for devas and humans."

The eyes and ears must discern right from wrong. It is like a bird flying through the sky with its wings broken; it is like an arrow shot at a target with its string severed. Because the string is severed, the target is not hit;
because the wings are broken, flight through the sky is impossible. When the string is strong and the wings are firm, both the sky and the target are penetrated.
How is it that these ten wisdoms are identical to the Truth? Let me point them out for you, Venerable Elders: first, they share the same substance.
Second, sharing the great matter; third, collectively participating in the investigation; fourth, sharing true wisdom; fifth, sharing universal pervasiveness;
sixth, sharing complete fulfillment; seventh, sharing gain and loss; eighth, sharing life and death; ninth, sharing the roar of the voice; tenth, sharing entry. It is further asked:
With what kind of person does one share entry? With whom does one share the roar of the voice? What is meant by sharing life and death? What is it?
All things share the same gain and loss; with whom do they equally possess [this]? What is this that is equally pervasive? Who possesses the same true wisdom?
Who can fully participate in this common practice? Who shares the same great matter? What thing shares the same substance?
Is there anyone who can point it out? To those who can point it out, I shall not withhold my compassion. But for those who cannot point it out, they have yet to possess the eye of study.
"You must by all means discern and recognize the true face of right and wrong. It is unacceptable to leave this matter unresolved for long. Take care. The letter continued:
"When the voices of all people throughout the universe reach this point, they are shattered into a hundred fragments.
Qian said, 'One should not follow him merely because he plays the flute; one should also strike the great drum to accompany him.'"
The forty-fourth patriarch, Chan Master Shishuang Chuyuan, was born into the Li clan of Qingxiang in Quanzhou. In his youth, he was a scholar.

At the age of twenty-two, he received the full precepts at Yinjing Temple on Mount Xiang south of the city. His mother was a woman of virtuous conduct and encouraged him to travel to study under various masters.
The Master had joined eyebrows and prominent eyes; he was tall and robust, yet he did not conform to conventional standards of decorum wherever he went.

He was rebuked by an elderly senior for being too young in his monastic experience. The Master laughed with a voice like a cliff crashing against brushwood, saying, "The trampling of dragons and elephants is not something a donkey can endure.
He once carried a chest of miscellaneous relics in a bag, slung over his shoulder on a bamboo staff, as he traveled between Xiangyang and Mian.
Together with Shou, they formed a companion group and entered Luoyang, where they heard that Chan Master Fenyang Shanzhao’s reputation for the Way was preeminent throughout the land.

First: Resolute Determination and Reliance on the Master. At that time, the imperial court was in the midst of launching a punitive expedition against Hedong, and heavy troops were stationed in Lu and Ze prefectures.
Many urged him not to go, but the Master paid them no heed. He crossed the Great River and ascended Mount Taihang; he changed his clothes and waited for an opportunity, while his attendants fled.
He was known as the Fire Company. Sleeping in the open and lodging among the grass, he eventually reached Longzhou and went to see Fenyang Wuye.

Master Zhao esteemed him, yet for two years he did not permit him to enter his inner quarters. The Master visited Zhao, who, sensing his resolve, would invariably respond with insults and abuse toward his attendants, or disparage the various masters of other regions;
whatever instructions he gave were all mundane and vulgar matters. One night, the Master petitioned him, saying: "Since arriving at your Dharma hall..."
The meal was finished. For two more summers, he received no instruction; instead, his worldly and defiled thoughts only increased.

As the years slipped by, he remained unclear regarding his own fundamental task and lost the benefit of his renunciation. Before he had even finished speaking, Master Zhao stared at him intently and scolded him, saying, "You are a wicked teacher!
How dare you deceive and exploit me? In a fit of rage, he raised his staff to drive him away. The Master prepared to intervene and rescue him, but Master Zhao covered his mouth. The Master—
Dawu said, "Thus I know that Linji’s Way transcends ordinary sentiment. Having served him for seven years, he took his leave and went to rely upon Chan Master Tangming Song.
Song said to him, "The Imperial Secretary Yang Dainian possesses high insight and his reputation is well-established;
you must certainly go see him. Thereupon, the Master went to visit Dainian. Dainian asked, "We face one another, yet I do not recognize you. From a thousand li..."
[Zhao] Zhe replied, "It is just like the wind. The Master said, "I have recently received an invitation from the Mountain Gate (the monastery).
[Zhao] Zhe said, "That is truly a fabrication. The Master said, "I left Tangming last month. [Zhao] Zhe said, "Now I regret having asked you. The Master said, "An adept! [Zhao] Zhe gave a shout.

The Master said, "Exactly so! [Zhao] Zhe shouted again. The Master made a sweeping gesture with his hand. [Zhao] Zhe stuck out his tongue and said, "Truly a dragon and an elephant! The Master said, "Indeed."
"What kind of talk is this? Daian looked back and had him serve tea separately, saying, "It turns out you are a member of my own household. The Master said, "That is unnecessary.
After a long silence, Daian asked again, "What is the phrase for helping others used by Yuan Zuo? The Master said, "The blade. (Qie).
Minister Nian said, "A true master! A true master! The Master replied, "I grant you, Inner Secretary, twenty blows of the staff.
Minister Nian tapped his knee and said, "What kind of place is this? The Master clapped his hands and said, "You must not let him go. Minister Nian laughed heartily.
He asked again, "Do you remember the circumstances regarding Tang Ming’s realization? The Master replied, "Tang Ming heard a monk ask Shoushan about the Buddha-dharma."
Yanyi said, "On the outskirts of King Chu’s city, the Ru River flows eastward. Yanguan asked, "Regarding the meaning of these words, how would you explain them?
The Master said, "A lantern hanging over the water. Yanguan said, "If that is so, then you have failed the ancients.
The Master said, "If you, Inner Secretary, have doubts, then seek another teacher. Yanguan said, "A three-legged frog leaps into the sky. The Master said, "Do as you please."

Hui-pao leaped up and laughed heartily. He was lodged in the meditation hall, where he questioned him regarding the principles of the Dharma from morning until evening. Upon hearing of the former words and past deeds of his predecessors, Hui-zheng lamented that he had met him so late in life.
When he saw the Prince of the Household (Fu-ma Du-wei), Li Gong, he said, "I have recently encountered a Way-man who is truly a lion of the West River.
Li Gong replied, "I am constrained by official regulations and cannot go to visit him; what can be done? Da...
He returned home in silence that year and said to his master, "Lord Li is a follower of the Buddha-dharma; having heard that the wind of your Way has reached afar, he has a desire to see you.
It is simply because the Dharma does not permit me to accompany you as an attendant that I have come alone. At dawn the next day, the Master went to visit Lord Li.
Lord Li read the visiting card and sent a pageboy to inquire about the Master's attainment before granting him an audience with the Head Seat. The Master said, "I have come specifically today."
They looked at one another. He then told the attendant boy, "When the inscription on the stele is carved in white characters, plant green pines along the road.
The Master said, "If it were not for this festival day, such an occasion would surely be difficult to encounter on other days. The boy came forward again and said, "The Commandant says:
'In that case, I shall go to meet you, Venerable Sir. The Master said, "From head to foot. Li Gong then emerged, sat down, and questioned him.
Li said, "I have heard that there is a golden-haired lion in the West River—is this true? The Master asked, "Where did you get such news?
Li gave a shout. The Master said, "A jackal howling. Li shouted again. The Master said, "Exactly so. Li laughed heartily.
Having taken his leave, Li asked for a single phrase to take with him as he departed. The Master said, "Take good care of yourself. Li said, "How is this different from other places?
The Master asked, "What about you, Excellency? Li replied, "I would give the Senior Monk twenty blows. The Master said, "That was specifically for the sake of its circulation."
Li shouted again. The Master said, "Blind! Li said, "Go well. The Master said, "Yes, yes. From then on, he came and went between the gates of Yang and Li, taking the Dharma as his friend.
After some time, he took his leave to return to Hedong. Li asked, "Is there a single phrase you can entrust to Tang Ming?
The Master said, "The bright moon shines upon the traveler at night. Li said, "That does not quite fit. The Master said, "Furthermore..."
"Profound, it is still tolerable; yet after midday, it causes one further anxiety. Nian asked, "Why has the Vajra before Kaibō Temple recently broken into a sweat?
The Master said, "I know. Nian asked, "As you are about to depart, Senior, do you have no word for the benefit of others? The Master said:
On the mountain pass of Chongdie, Nan’an said, “In that case, I shall follow you, Venerable. The Master made a sighing sound. Nan’an said, “A true lion cub.

When the Master returned to Tang China, Lord Li sent two monks to inquire after him. At the end of his letter, the Master drew a pair of feet and wrote the names of the visiting monks to send them back.
Lord Li composed a verse, which said: “The black brush has traveled more than a thousand li.”
The golden coffin revealed his twin footprints; humans and devas were utterly unable to fathom it. Cherish this red-bearded barbarian! The Master, because his mother was elderly, returned south.
Upon arriving at Junzhou, he led the assembly of monks at Dongshan at a time when Chan Master Cong resided there. Previously, Fenyang had said to the Master:
"I have traveled everywhere to study under the elders and descendants of Yunmen, yet I have specifically harbored regret for not having seen Cong. Therefore...

The Master remained in reliance for three years and then traveled to Mount Yang. Yang Dainian sent a letter to Huang Zongdan, the Governor of Yichun, requesting that he invite the Master to take charge of a monastery and preach the Dharma.
The Governor vacated Nan Yuan for him, but the Master did not go. He subsequently went specifically to visit the Governor and expressed his wish to travel.
When the Governor asked the reason for this, he replied, "At first it was out of deference; now I simply wish to go. The Governor was greatly impressed.
He esteemed him. After staying for three years, he departed and went to pay his respects to Chan Master Dingyin of Shoushan.

Dingyin was a senior disciple of Shishuang, held in high esteem, and at that time, among the monastics, none who were not of extraordinary refinement dared to enter his gate. He had resided on the mountain for thirty years, and his disciples’ reputation overwhelmed all other quarters.
The Master [Fenyang] did not cut his hair long, wore tattered robes, and spoke with a Chu accent; when he came to announce his arrival, he addressed himself as follows:
"Brother-in-law of the Dharma! the entire assembly laughed loudly. Yìn sent a young attendant to ask the Elder, "Whose successor are you?

The Master looked up at the roof and said, "I have seen Fenyang in person. Yìn came out leaning on his staff; seeing the Master’s tall and imposing figure, he asked, "Is there a 'Lion of West River' in Fenzhou?
The Master pointed behind him and cried out, "The roof is collapsing! The attendant fled backward, and Yìn [turned back].
Looking back, he saw Xue-shuo sitting on the ground; having removed one sandal, he gazed at him. The old man Yan forgot what he had asked and also lost sight of where the Master was.
The Master slowly rose, adjusted his robes, and as he walked away, said: "Seeing the person is not as good as hearing of their reputation."
He then departed. Yuanren sent someone to pursue him, but it was to no avail. He sighed and said, "Fenzhou has such a son!

From that time on, the Master’s reputation grew weighty within the monastic community. The śramaṇa Benyan of Dinglin possessed noble spiritual practice and was trusted and revered by scholars and officials.
When Yuanren met Benyan, he praised the Master’s insight, saying, "He can revive Linji. At that time, the seat at Daowu was vacant, so Yuanren [invited] Benyan...
He petitioned the Prefect to appoint him as the abbot. His administration was strict and orderly, and those who would sacrifice their lives for the Dharma gathered there.
Throughout his life, the Master practiced the conduct of non-obstruction in all things, such that neither ordinary beings nor sages could fathom it.

While sitting in meditation within his quarters, he placed a sword horizontally across a water basin and set a straw sandal beside it, requiring those who came to inquire about the Way to provide a response; yet none were able to accord with his standard.
Ji said: "It would be better to stop, to rest; let body and mind become simple and sincere. Yao Fengqian remarked:
"This is the numinous power of the Indian patriarchs; it grows like iron flowers upon the summit of Shuangfeng Peak."
The forty-fifth patriarch, Chan Master Yangqi Fanghui, was born into the Li family. He was a native of Yichun in Yuanzhou.

From his youth, he was alert and quick-witted, possessing a humorous and witty manner of speech that was full of flavor. Upon reaching adulthood, he took no pleasure in the study of writing or ink-stones; instead, he registered himself under the name of a merchant tax official to manage the collection of duties.

Once, while presiding over his post, he was found negligent and was due for punishment. He fled by night and traveled to Jiufeng in Junzhou, where he suddenly attained a state of profound realization.

At his former place of practice, his attendants could not bear to leave him, so he shaved his head and became a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*). There, he read the sutras and listened to the Dharma until his mind was harmonized and his spirit attained realization.
He was able to humble himself with great earnestness and relied upon the venerable elder Chan Master Ciming, residing at Nan-yuan.

The Master assisted him, and he lived in peace while applying himself to diligent toil. When Ciming moved to Dao-wu and Shi-shuang, the Master accompanied him and requested to take charge of the community.

The matter of serving as the *jianyuan* (superintendent) was not in accordance with Ciming’s intention, yet the assembly clamored in favor of it. Carrying his paper quilt, he entered to oversee the treasury;

from time to time, he would speak bluntly, chiding and correcting Ciming. The various quarters of the Buddhist world circulated the view that this was appropriate, and although he remained in that position for a long time, they followed him accordingly.
However, he had not yet attained awakening. He went to consult Master Ming every day, but Ming would say, "The affairs of the administrative office are many;
go for now. On another day, when he asked again, Ming said, "In time, your disciples and descendants will fill the world;
why be so busy? One day, as Ming happened to go out, it suddenly began to rain. The Master scouted him on a small path, and upon seeing him, he grabbed him and said, "This old fellow, today..."
"You must tell me; I will not beat you. Ming said, "The Prior knows this sort of thing, so let it be.
Before he had finished speaking, the Master attained great enlightenment. He immediately prostrated himself on the muddy ground and asked, "When meeting on a narrow path, what then?
Ming said, "You should step aside; I have somewhere I must go. On his return day, the Master assumed the full ceremonial regalia and went to the Abbot’s quarters.
"Venerable Sir," [the master] said, bowing in thanks. Ming-ho rebuked him, saying, "Not yet. After eating his meal, Ciming would invariably go for walks in the mountains;
when practitioners of Chan asked about the Way, they often lost his whereabouts. Seeing that he had not been gone long, the Master (Fenyang) immediately beat the drum to assemble the assembly.

Ciming hurried back and scolded him, counting off his faults: "In the monasteries of the past, one did not ascend the seat until evening; where did you get this rule? The Master replied slowly, "At Fén..."
This was the evening assembly of the Prefectural Governor. Ciming was at his wits' end. When Ciming moved to Xinghua, the Master took his leave and returned to Pingshi on Mount Jiufeng.
Laypeople and monks went to the mountain and requested that he take up residence at Yangqi.

At that time, the Elder Qin of Jiufeng did not know the Master; surprised, he asked, "Does the Prior Hui also practice Chan? The Master accepted the formal invitation, and after the question-and-answer session was concluded, he said: "Furthermore..."
"Is there anyone who can speak? Come forth and meet me! Yangqi’s life today rests in your hands;
you may drag him about and pull him down as you please. Why? Because a man of true stature must be tested and judged in public.
Do not act like one pressing a gourd underwater in secret; let us examine and verify him before the assembly. Look and see if there is anyone!"
"Ma! If there were no Yangqi, you would have lost out. As he descended from his seat, Wukong held him firmly and said, "Today I am truly glad to have found a fellow practitioner.
The Master asked, "What is this matter of being a 'fellow practitioner'? Wukong replied, "Yangqi is plowing with the ox; Jiufeng is pulling the harrow."

The Master said, "At this very moment, Yangqi is here before me; Jiufeng is here before me; Qinqiu is speechless. The Master pushed them aside and said, "I thought they were fellow practitioners, but it turns out they are not.
They are merely those whose names are heard in all quarters. He ascended the hall and said: "Yangqi has just settled in;
the walls of the house are thin. The entire bed is covered with snow and pearls. One must shrink one's neck and sigh in dark sorrow. After a long silence, he spoke again.
He said: "I recall the ancients dwelling beneath trees; when asked in the meditation hall about the 'thorny chestnut' (*liji pong*), how would you respond?
Regarding the 'diamond ring' (*jingang quan*) that one must swallow, how would you penetrate it?"
The inscription reads: "I respectfully present this one text as a token of gratitude for the future. Yao Fengqian remarked: "Brilliant as the sun and stars.
The forty-sixth patriarch, Chan Master Baoyun Shouduan, was born into the Ge clan in Hengzhou; from his youth, he was skilled in calligraphy.
He took no pleasure in remaining among the laity and went to Chaling Master Yu to receive the tonsure. When he was over twenty years old, he visited Chan Master Yong;
after Yong passed away, Master Hui succeeded him in residence there. One day, the Master marveled at him and would often converse with him until late into the night.

One day, during a private interview, Yuanwu cited a scriptural passage, saying: "When seeing sees, that which sees is not the seeing; even seeing is already apart from seeing. Seeing does not...
Nengji raised his fist and asked, "Do you see it? The Master replied, "I see it. Yuanwu said, "Placing a head upon a head. At these words, the Master attained a realization.
Yuanwu asked again, "What have you seen? The Master replied, "The dense bamboo does not hinder the flowing water from passing through."
Yuanwu approved of him. He was soon appointed to oversee the library. When someone asked about this, Yuanwu said, "How can a Librarian Director as gentle and compliant as Long accomplish anything?
Yuanwu replied, "He is a sleeping tiger. From then on, he followed Yuanwu like a shadow follows a form for twenty years.
With relentless searching and probing, he fully mastered Yuanwu’s secrets. Because his parents had grown old with white hair, the Master returned home.
He resided at Baoshan in his native prefecture. Subsequently, he accepted an invitation to dwell at Kaisheng Temple west of the city.

During the chaos of the Jianyan era, he built a thatched hut at the foot of Tongfeng Peak. Prefect Li Gongguang invited him to reside at Zhangjiao, and later he moved to Huqiu. His Way became widely renowned.
Consequently, following the precedent of Master Baiyun Dan, he established a Patriarchs Hall, saying: "To act for the sake of others..."
Later, [the Master] lamented, "If I cannot personally practice the bequeathed instructions, how can I find peace in their meaning? He subsequently had an image of him painted to offer his veneration.

At that time, as the times were not yet settled, Yuanwu traveled down the Gorges to return to Sichuan. Those younger disciples who had previously flocked to him like rivers rushing toward the sea all turned their gaze toward the mountain and hurried there.
Whenever the Master ascended the seat, he revealed the Dharma with composure; it was of a single, equal flavor, and according to the capacities of those present, all were satisfied.
Because of his desire [to propagate the Dharma], Yuanwu’s Way was once again widely disseminated throughout the various regions of the southeast, as if Yuanwu were still present.
[One day] he ascended the hall. A monk asked, "When the ancients reached this point, why did they refuse to stay? The Master said, "I, the old monk, am just like that.
The monk asked, "What happens when one suddenly cuts them in two with a single stroke? The Master said, "A god walking on level ground."
The inscription reads: "Requiting both requited and unrequited kindness. Yao Fengqian wrote: "Fragrant breezes cling to the robe-sleeves.
The fiftieth patriarch, Chan Master Ying’an Tanhua, was born into the Jiang family; he was a native of Huangmei in Qi.

From childhood, he was extraordinary and outstanding, with a prominent and elegant physique. Even as a youth, he grew weary of worldly affairs. At the age of seventeen, he left home to become a monk at Dong [Monastery] in his hometown.
Chan. The following year he became a full monk (*bhikṣu*). The year after that, he traveled with his mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*) to visit various teachers.

He first called upon Master Sui of Suinan in Suizhou, where he tasted the flavor of the Dharma. He traveled extensively throughout the south and north of Lake Dongting and the east and west of the Yangtze River;

wherever he went, he engaged in vigorous debate with the elder masters, finding perfect accord with them all. He ascended to Yunju to pay respects to Chan Master Yuanwu, who, upon seeing him, greeted him with an embrace and exhorted him earnestly.
He was diligent and tireless, serving with such zeal that he feared only falling behind his peers. When Yuanwu entered Sichuan, he directed him to visit Zhangjiao Longxu;

when Longxu moved to Huqiu, the Master served as his vanguard. Within less than half a year, he had thoroughly penetrated the Great Dharma and suddenly attained a clear realization of Yuanwu’s teaching.
Yuanwu’s methods for training people were profound and firm, yet his application of them was vast and expansive; every word and phrase he uttered transcended conventional standards.
His reputation was vast and his fame resounded throughout the monastic communities. Before long, he took his leave and traveled to various regions.
Initially, he shared the teaching seat with Chushi Lianyun; when Chushi was succeeded by Miaoyan, he invited the Master to take charge of the monastery. Subsequently, he resided at Mingguo in Quzhou.
Qi’s Dezhang; Raoyang’s Ba’en and Jianfu; Wuzhou’s Baolin and Ba’en; Jiangxi’s Donglin; Jiankang’s Jiangshan;
Pingjiang’s Wanshou; twice residing at Nankang’s Guizong; and finally residing at Tiantong.
He opened the gate of great giving and extended his hand to those who had not yet awakened. From near and far, people flocked to him like water rushing into a ravine. At Puguang...

The small-scale sermons (*xiaocan*), question-and-answer sessions, and formal examinations he delivered were all characterized by a relaxed and leisurely composure, executed with the utmost skillful means (*upāya*).

His spontaneous wit and discernment within the meditation hall—his mastery over the deployment of "killing" and "giving life"—were particularly renowned for their brilliance and subtlety. Even those who had studied extensively and undergone rigorous training would break into a cold sweat and feel their spirits wither the moment they approached his mallet and whisk, lamenting that they had encountered him too late.
They would then exert themselves with sincere intent to accomplish what was otherwise difficult to assemble, thereby offering their report of gratitude and service.

Formerly, those who led disciples and presided over monasteries all concealed their names and traces, considering it a great fortune merely to have a place to set down their robes and bowls in the lower ranks.
Ascending the hall, [he said]: "Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are without obstruction; sound, fragrance, taste, and touch are always in samādhi.
Seeing with the eyes is like being blind; speaking with the mouth is like being mute. People of Suzhou are dull-witted; people of Changzhou wander the wilds. Within the Great Song Empire..."
There were only two monks: one from Sichuan and one from Zhejiang; all the others were "sons"—sons of Huainan, sons of Jiangxi, sons of Guangnan, and sons of Fujian.
Have you not heard it said: "The father is compassionate and the son is filial; the Way is contained therein"?

The inscription states: "Looking at the present through the lens of the past, one severs the rush of worldly distractions. Yao Fengqian remarked: "The ancient trees and old family home are observed by all from every quarter.
The fifty-first patriarch, Chan Master Mian Xianjie, was the son of the Zheng clan of Fuzhou. His mother dreamed of Mount Lu...

This old monk was born into a common household. From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and keen-witted. He left home to become a monk and, undaunted by the hardships of travel, went everywhere to consult various masters of the Way.
Later, he visited Ying’an at Mingguo Monastery in Quzhou. Because his character was solitary and rigid, it was difficult for him to gain entry;
he was repeatedly rebuked. One day, the Master asked, "What is the Eye of the True Dharma? The Teacher immediately replied, "A broken sand pot. Ying’an nodded his head in approval. Not long after...

He made several polite excuses to return home to visit his parents. The Hermit sent him off with this verse: "The phrase of great penetration that strikes the vital point— The crown of the head is opened wide in the presence of reality.

We have followed one another for four years now; In our mutual inquiry, not a trace remains. Though the dharma-bowl has not yet been entrusted to you, Your spirit and bearing swallow up heaven and earth."
Yet he took the True Dharma Eye and called it a broken sand-pot. On this journey to pay his respects, take care not to set up a fixed root.
I have a final word; wait until you return, and I shall require you to follow it. He entered the world at Quji, then moved successively to Xiangfu, Jiangshan, and Huazang.
Not long after, by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Jingshan and Lingyin. In his later years, he dwelt at Taibai. [One day] he ascended the hall and said: "One..."
A gourd has just fallen to the ground; gourds everywhere lie overturned. If you wish to recognize the Chan of direct transmission and pointing directly, today’s assembly is perfectly suited for it.
The Preface states: "Advancing must be done with propriety; retreating must be done with propriety. Yao enfeoffed Qian, saying:
"I dare not point with my finger.
The fifty-second patriarch, Chan Master Pō'ān Zuān, was born in the Wang family of Guǎng'ān in Shū. He followed Luóhàn...

Yuan Dexiang left the household life. Hearing that the elder master Yuan was residing at Zhaojue, he went there to seek instruction. Their words were in accord, and Yuan was ordered to serve as the successor to Yuanwu’s incense and offerings.
One day, as he was passing before the abbot’s quarters, Yuan asked, "Is there anyone in the hermitage? The Master replied, "No one.

Before Yuan had finished speaking, he struck him across the chest with a fist and said, "What about you? The Master suddenly attained realization. He then left the valley and relied upon [the master].

De Shan Juan of Liuzhou shaved his head and soon thereafter received full ordination. He traveled extensively to visit various masters throughout the land until he reached Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou.
One snowy night, while sitting in meditation, he thought to himself, "I have been traveling as a pilgrim for ten years, yet I still cannot attain thorough penetration.

While he was in a state of deep frustration, he did not notice the bell tolling; as he went toward the rear hall, he looked up and saw the two characters "Zhao Tang" (Hall of Illumination). His doubts were instantly resolved. Subsequently, he...
At Shuanglin, Shuian asked, "Why does the bearded man of the Western Heaven have no beard? The Master said, "Were it not for Shuanglin, this story would not be brought up.
Shuian said, "Today I have run into a true adept. The Master said, "The heart bears no grudge against others;
the face shows no shame. Shuian then stepped back. The Master said, "You have been seen through. When Shuian reached... [the text continues].
Having retired from his duties at An, he went to see Mian at Wugu. Mian appointed the Master as the guest prefect. One day, while Mian was conversing with a monk nearby, he raised the koan:
"It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. Upon hearing this, the Master attained a sudden and great awakening.
The following day, Mian encountered the Master before the monks' quarters and said to him, "In no way may you employ any artifice. Try to reveal some sign of your realization."
"Look," the Master replied at the sound of the voice. "There is a guest in the abbot’s quarters. He laughed heartily. Later, when Foyan moved to Jiangshan, the Master attended him on his travels.

They remained together for five years, during which time he fully mastered the essential points of the teaching. Taking his leave to return to Sichuan, Foyan sent him off with this verse: The old man has long since passed away; The mountain road is steep and difficult to traverse. If you wish to see the true man, Do not look back at the old traces.

Coming from ten thousand *li* to the south, he crossed the river at Chuanyu. With a rushing torrent as sharp as a blade, he struck the profound pivot; the *zhizhi* at the crown of his head blinded the Vajra-eye.
His coming and going were like a pearl rolling across a tray. Subsequently, he traveled south to Kuimen, where the Minister Yang Gongfu invited him to reside at Wolong.
He declined and departed, traveling extensively through Wu to visit Huizang Dun’an Yan and Jinnshan Tui’an.
Qi Lingyin Xianan Wu and Jingshan Mongan Cong were both appointed as First Seat (Dìyīzuò) and charged with preaching the Dharma.
They subsequently resided at Jianfu in Changzhou, Lingyan in Zhenzhou, Xiufeng and Qionglong in the Wu region, and at the request of Prince Yang, they took up residence at Zifu in Huzhou.
Later, Layman Zhang Yuozhai invited them to serve as the founding patriarch (Kāishān) of Guangshou Huyun Chan Monastery.
While presiding over six seats of the Dharma assembly, he ascended the hall and said: "What is Chan? It is the Jambū tree at the edge of the southern continent of Jambudvīpa.

It supports the heavens and props up the earth; it props up the earth and supports the heavens. It cannot be described through clever words; it requires only transmission from mind to mind. Ultimately, what is this 'Chan, Chan'?"
The memorial stated: "Select one senior monk (*upādhyāya*) who has mastered the Sanskrit of the Five Indias. Yao Feng Qian said:
"Blowing fire with a long, pointed beak.
The fifty-third patriarch, Chan Master Shifan of Mount Jing, was born in Zizhong of Shu into the Yong clan. Nine...

In his youth, he followed Master Daoqin on Mount Yinping and left the household life. Upon merely glancing at the scriptures, he could recite them from memory. In the fifth year of the Shaohui era, he received full ordination.
He traveled abroad until reaching Chengdu, where he spent the summer retreat at Zhengfa Temple. There was an elder, the head seat Yao, who was a high-ranking disciple of Xia Tang.
The Master requested instruction on the method of seated meditation (zazen). Yao asked, "What is this 'meditation' (chan)? Who is it that sits?
The Master took these words to heart and investigated them day and night. One day, while using the toilet, he attained realization regarding the previous dialogue and took his leave.
He went to rely upon Fozhao at the East Hermitage of Yuyang. Fozhao asked, "Where are you from? The Master replied, "From Jianzhou. Fozhao said, "Did you bring your sword with you?"
"Are you coming? The Master let out a shout as soon as the voice fell. Zhao laughed and said, "This fellow with the black head is acting recklessly.

Because he was so impoverished that he lacked the funds to shave his hair, people called him "Black Head" (Wutouzi). Not long after, hearing that Pō'ān was residing at Xīhuà Xiùfēng in Sūzhōu, Zhao went there to see him.
When a man named Chūndián entered the room, he met Pō'ān with a bold and unyielding challenge; Pō'ān struck him.
They arrived at the Dharma Hall, intending to expel him. The Master explained it to them, saying, "For practitioners of Chan, it is but a common occurrence to contend over meditation;
why must you go so far as this? The Hermit said, "Have you not heard the saying: 'When my belly is hungry, hearing the sound of the wooden board, I want to go eat rice'?"
When the Master heard these words, he was so startled that cold sweat broke out across his back. Later, when Pò’ān served as the First Seat at Línghyìn, [Zhìzēng] went to follow him once again.
While attending Pò’ān, they visited Shíshǔn Ān. A practitioner there requested instruction, saying, "The monkey-child cannot be caught;
I beg the Master for a skillful means. Pò’ān said, "What is the use of trying to catch it? It is like wind blowing over water."

The characters formed themselves naturally. As the Master stood by his side, the burden that had long obstructed his chest was suddenly released. He resided in a nest among the clouds on Mount Qionglong in Wu County;
later, he moved to Ruiwang and then to Ruiyan in Taizhou, where both monasteries invited him to share the teaching seat.

While the Master was at Ruiyan, he suddenly dreamed of a person in magnificent robes and cap who presented him with a handful of wild grass. The following day, a special messenger arrived from Qingyuan in Mingzhou.
Upon entering the monastery, he saw the guardian deity of the temple; his surname was Mao, and his attire and appearance were no different from what he had previously seen in his dream.
He subsequently moved to Mount Jiao and ascended to Xuedou, where he was successively commanded by imperial decree to transfer to Yewang and later to Jing Mountain.

The Master resided at Jing Mountain for twenty years; his stores were abundant and his assembly as vast as the sea. Although the monastery suffered two disasters of fire, it was soon restored to its former state.

Observation. The reputation of this Dharma assembly was at its peak. [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "If one were to discuss this matter, it is straightforward, essential, and easy to understand.
Yet most of you create difficulties for yourselves and erect obstacles for yourselves.
Therefore, sometimes when I see people on the eastern or western corridors bowing in greeting, I simply lower my head in response. In truth, there is nothing else; I simply wish to..."
The people recognized him. The Elder was a native of Longqing Prefecture in Xichuan.
The inscription reads: "Reflecting upon the place of good fortune, it lies beyond words. Yao Fengqian remarked:
"Cast away and scattered, he was mixed among the sands and stones."
The fifty-fourth patriarch was Zen Master Yangshan Zuqin, a native of Wuzhou. He became a monk at the age of sixteen and began his travels as a mendicant at eighteen.
Having heard that Master Tianmu had long served Songyuan and was thus Songyuan’s dharma heir, he was certain that Tianmu would possess Songyuan’s discourse style.
He went to Jingci Monastery with incense in his sleeve to seek instruction; Tianmu specifically showed him the karmic conditions concerning Huangbo’s reception of Linji. Furthermore—
[The Master] said: "When Huìyuán resided on this mountain, I went there for a brief visit and entered his room. He said, 'This is a case already resolved;
even before you have stepped through the gate, I have already given you thirty blows. You should simply look at it in this way.

At that time, the Master had not yet grasped its meaning and said, "Ordinarily, when I request instruction, at the conclusion there is one stick of incense and three prostrations, which is called 'thanking for the karmic conditions.'"
This single stick of incense of mine has not yet been consumed; as before, I have applied my own effort and sat in meditation for three years without my side touching the mat.
One day, as soon as I mounted the meditation cushion, it was suddenly as if the earth had collapsed beneath me.

From then on, I remained in a state of pure nakedness for over half a month, and no movement-phenomena arose. However, during the middle of the night, I fell asleep without dreams, without thoughts, and without [consciousness].
Hearing of the ground of non-seeing, they further split it into two fragments. They can understand the sayings and phrases of the ancients that follow the path of principle;
however, when encountering what is like a silver mountain or an iron wall, they fail to comprehend them at all.

Although the Master had long been under the guidance of Wuzu Fayan at Mount Jing, whenever he entered the room for instruction—even upon reaching the "fangers and claws" of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—he was invariably at a loss for words. Thus it was.
For ten years he traveled through eastern Zhejiang. One day, while walking before the Buddha Hall, he raised his eyes and saw a great cypress tree;
that which had long been a thorn in his side suddenly dispersed. He visited Wuzhun at Mount Jing and, because Wuzhun was casting a bell, requested him to compose a preface for it.
The Master composed a verse, saying: "The entire body is but a single mouth, Rolled out from within a furnace of a hundred refinements. Severing..."
After seeing off the setting sun, he again urged the rising moon onto the towers and terraces. Zhun immediately appointed him to the position of Attendant.

From then on, his reputation resounded throughout the monastic communities. He took up residence at Longxing Temple in Tanzhou, was subsequently transferred to Daolin in Xiangxi, and finally to Furi in Chuzhou.
At Husheng in Taizhou and Guangxiao in Huzhou, and upon reaching Yangshan, his Way flourished greatly.
He ascended the hall and said: "Upon one seeing, you see; upon one attaining, you attain forever. Extending his hands, he said: "Open both hands and everyone look!
Ultimately, what is this luminous thing? In the inner and outer parts of Tanzhou, there were eighteen city gates, where travelers passed by during the day.
"Millions upon millions, coming and going, free to roam in the east, west, south, and north.
The Preface states: "He has swept away all reflective discernment; his phrasing and tone are so carefree and unencumbered that from this day forward, nothing can be predicted of him.
Yao Fengqian remarked: "His 'broken hairpin' curves are superior to the 'leakage trace' of the eaves."
The fifty-fifth patriarch, Zen Master Tianmu Yuanmiao, was a native of Wujiang. His surname was Xu and his mother’s was Zhou. She conceived him after dreaming of a monk arriving by boat.
He was born in the *wuxu* year of the Jiaxi era of the Song dynasty (1238). From infancy, he delighted in sitting in the lotus posture and felt a deep affection for monks.
At the age of fifteen, he earnestly requested his parents’ permission to leave the household life and entered Miaoyin Temple in Jiahe.
16. He remained in the Dharma. 17. He shaved his head. 18. He received full ordination. 19. He studied the teachings of Tiantai. 20.

He changed his robes and entered Jingci Monastery, where he established a three-year limit for himself to study Chan meditation. One day, his father and elder brother arrived; he sat there with dignified composure, paying them no heed.

The twenty-second [case] concerns Jiandu Qiaolun. He instructed his fellow practitioners to contemplate from where one comes at birth and where one goes at death, until both speech and body were forgotten.
At times, he would leave the latrine wearing only his inner robe; at other times, he would open a letter case and depart without noticing the lock.

On one occasion, his fellow practitioner Xian sighed with regret, saying, "I am unable to accomplish my own task; how can I not assist him so that he may achieve success? Thus, he guarded [Qiaolun] day and night.
He attended with the utmost reverence. At that time, Zen Master Xueyan Qin was residing at Beijian Pagoda. With joyful anticipation, he went there carrying incense to seek instruction;

as soon as he offered his greetings, the master struck him out and shut the door. Only after going back a second time did he finally gain access. He was then instructed to contemplate the "Mu" (No) koan.
From then on, he engaged in inquiry without a single day of negligence. Whenever Qin asked, "Who is it that drags this corpse here? before the sound had even faded—
Jue struck him immediately. Qin went to Nanming; the Master then ascended Mount Shuangjing. Suddenly, while in a dream, he recalled the dialogue raised in Duanqiao’s room:
"All dharmas return to One—where does that One return? A state of doubt suddenly arose within him. For three days and nights, his eyes did not close.
On a day coinciding with the memorial service for Shaolin, he joined the assembly at the Three Pagodas. While chanting the sutras, he looked up and suddenly beheld—
The Fifth Patriarch, Master Yuan, offered this eulogy for his portrait: "A hundred years, thirty-six thousand mornings; turning back and forth, it is always just this fellow.
Suddenly, one breaks through the doubt of 'dragging a corpse'. At the conclusion of the summer retreat, the Master went to visit Nanming Qin.
Upon seeing him, [Nanming] immediately asked, "Who gave you this corpse to drag here? The Master then shouted. Nanming raised his staff; the Master seized it.
Zhuzhu said, "Today I cannot strike this person. Qin asked, "Why can you not strike him? The Master shook his sleeves and departed.

From then on, his spiritual sharpness was such that he would not yield. The following year, he spent the summer retreat at Jiangxin. Traveling by way of Guoqing, he passed through Xuedou and met Xiwei Mou.
He stayed as a guest in the hall with Hiseu Tan, who asked, "Where have you come from? The Master cast [his staff].

He struck down the meditation cushion. Dan asked, "Regarding the dog's Buddha-nature, how do you understand it? The Master said, "I cast it out for everyone to see. Dan personally escorted him back to the hall.
Later, when Dan hung up his plaque at Daochang and began teaching at Tianning, the Master attended upon him and performed his duties.
One day, Dan asked, "In the midst of the vast bustle of the day, are you still able to be the master? The Master said:
"Can one maintain mastery? He asked again, "In a dream, can one maintain mastery? The Master said, "One maintains mastery.
He asked again, "When one is fast asleep, without dreams, without thoughts, without seeing, and without hearing—where is the master? The Master was speechless.
Yunquan said, "From this day forward, you need not study the Buddha or the Dharma; you need not investigate the ancients."
Now, I simply eat when hungry and sleep when weary. As soon as I awaken, I rouse my spirit and ask:
"Where, ultimately, does this master of mine reside? Where does he establish his dwelling and sustain his life?
In the winter of the Bingyin year, I resolved to enter Longxu in Lin’an and vowed to myself: "I shall devote my entire life to being a simpleton; I must by all means achieve this."

One morning, while [Zhaozhou] was at ease, his pillow fell to the floor as he shifted in bed with a companion who was staying with him overnight; upon hearing the sound, he attained a vast and sudden enlightenment.
He said to himself: "It is like the man from Sizhou seeing the Great Sage, or a traveler returning to his native village.
Originally, it is simply the person of former times, walking the same path as before. He remained at Longxu for nine years, binding together wood to make a hut, which was pierced by the wind.

Scorched by the sun, he wore but a single robe throughout both winter and summer; he used neither fan nor brazier. Daily he pounded pine needles to mix with his gruel, sustaining his life by these means alone.

Once, when snow accumulated until it buried his meditation cell for over ten days, the paths were blocked and all communication ceased; everyone believed him dead. When the snow cleared, they saw the Master sitting in the *nāga-paryaṅka* posture.
In the year Jiashu, he moved to Mount Shuangji in Wukang. Disciples gathered like clouds, and as the hermitage was too small to accommodate them, he cleared away its...
The most eminent ones dwell therein. In the spring of the *bingzi* year, while the multitude fled in all directions to avoid the military conflict, the Master alone bolted his gate.

When they returned to their posts and opened the door, he sat there as motionless as before. Consequently, the number of visitors increased until he was unable to attend to them all. This gave rise to the saying:

"With a staff slung across his shoulder, he did not look back at people, but went straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks. In the spring of the *jimao* year, he packed his belongings into a cloth bag and fled under the cover of night.

He proceeded directly to the shoulder of the western peak of Tianmu Mountain, where there was Lion Rock (*Siṃha-śilā*). Rising a thousand *ren* from the ground, its rocky crags stood like a forest of pillars.

The Master delighted in it and conceived the intention to spend the remainder of his life there. His disciples, including Fasheng and others, followed him in succession and thatched a grass hut for him.
Before long, the community gathered once more. The Master then constructed a stone cave to the west of the rock and fashioned a small chamber within it, following the shape of a boat.
The hall was half the height of a *zhang* and half the width of a *heng*. A "Gate of Death" was inscribed upon it. It was slippery above and muddy below;

wind and rain blew and swirled about it. He cut off all attendants and discarded all luxuries. He did not bathe his body nor shave his hair. Using a broken jar as a cauldron, he ate but once every two days, yet remained composed and at ease.

The cave was so steep that one could not ascend without a ladder; he removed the ladder and severed all means of access, so that even his disciples rarely beheld him. Thus, he established the "Three Gates" of discourse.
The Verifier of Students said: "A person of great ultimate realization is fundamentally liberated from birth and death; why, then, does the life-root (jīvitendriya) not yet sever?

The public cases (gong'an) of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are but a single principle; why, then, is there clarity and lack of clarity? A practitioner of great cultivation should follow the conduct of the Buddha; why, then, do they not observe the Vinaya?
When their responses do not accord with the truth, they shut their doors and refuse to receive visitors. [He then] issued a general summons for communal labor.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Zen does not lie in the practice of the Way; there is no need for awakening through movement or activity.
To act with the majesty of mountains and peaks, to rouse the bold fellow Meng Babang—yet even going about in such a manner, how can it compare to West Peak’s hauling stones and carrying earth?"
The memorial states: "Do not look at its flowers; eat only its fruit, and thus one may not lose its fundamental principle.
Yao said to Qian: "In deep mountains and vast marshes, dragons and snakes truly breed."

The fifty-sixth patriarch, Chan Master Mingben of Tianmu, was a native of Qiantang in Hangzhou. His secular surname was Sun. His mother dreamed that the Wayman Wumen placed a lantern inside a basket at her home;
the next day, the Master was born. His divine countenance was exceptionally extraordinary, endowed with the marks of a great man.
As soon as he could speak, he sang praises and chanted Buddhist hymns; all his play was entirely the work of the Buddha. At the age of nine, he lost his mother and began to study...

He ceased his studies of the *Analects* and *Mencius* before finishing their volumes. At the age of fifteen, he resolved to leave the household life. He prostrated before the Buddha and set fire to his own arm as an offering.

He observed the five precepts and daily recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. At night, he constantly practiced walking meditation; when exhausted, he would strike his head against a pillar.
He lived in seclusion near Lingdong Mountain, where he would often ascend its summit to practice *dhyāna* concentration.
Before reaching the age of twenty, while reading the *Chuan deng lu*, he came upon the passage where the girl Āmala asks Mañjuśrī:

"If one clearly knows the principle that birth is non-birth, why is it that one is still driven by the cycle of birth and death? He harbored a doubt regarding this. A śramaṇa named Mingshan directed him to go and consult Gaofeng.
Master Miao was stern and cold, not relying on courtesy or facial expressions; yet upon seeing [the Master], he was immediately delighted and wished to have him tonsured.
The Master did not consent, as his father’s command had not yet been fulfilled. Miao said, "It is permissible," and exhorted him by citing the story of Venerable Śāṇakavāsin.

Before long, the Master recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and upon reaching the passage concerning "shouldering the Tathāgata," he attained full understanding. He subsequently mastered the meanings of both internal (Buddhist) and external (secular) classics.

At the age of twenty-five, Qiu received the tonsure from Miaoxing at Shizi Yuan. The following year, he received full ordination. Another year later, while observing flowing water, he attained a realization.

He went to Miaoxing to seek certification, but Miaoxing drove him away with blows. At that time, there was a rumor circulating among the common people that the government was selecting young boys and girls.
The Master asked, "Suppose someone were to come and ask the Abbot for a young boy or girl; what would you do?"

"What did you do? Miaoyan replied, "I simply took a bamboo hairpin and gave it to him. At these words, the Master attained sudden and complete enlightenment; however, he remained submerged within the assembly, with no one recognizing his realization.
Miaoyan wrote a true eulogy and presented it to the Master, saying: "My appearance is inconceivable; even Buddhas and patriarchs cannot behold it."

Only to this unworthy son did he grant [his seal]; seeing that he had attained half of the nose, he sent his disciples to him. The Master then requested further instruction from the assembly, through which they came to know where to turn.
The monk Zizheng of Huai once asked Miaoxin about the relative merits of his various disciples. Miaoxin said, "As for the first, he is the head of the monastery."

I have only a partial understanding; it cannot be said that I am entirely ignorant. As for Master Yishou, he is indeed a mature bamboo from an old grove, though his joints may be bent sevenfold or eightfold.

Qu Tingfa of Songjiang has donated land to establish a temple at Lotus Peak, naming it Dajuezheng.

When Dêngchán Monastery was about to undergo a change of leadership, they offered it to the Master. The Master declined. Thereupon, as the positions of the Five Mountains remained vacant, the authorities sent letters repeatedly requesting him to accept;
yet the Master declined them all with great resolve. He went so far as to dwell among the grasses on remote cliffs and solitary islands, lodging amidst the waves.

He concealed his traces and withdrew from them; nevertheless, scholars from all directions—reaching as far north as the Dragon Desert (Longmo), south to the Six Zhao states, west to the land of Śāṇḍilya (Shendu), and east to Mount Bosang—wrapped their provisions and donned straw sandals, rushing from ten thousand *li* to converge upon the Master like spokes meeting at the hub, with not a single day passing without arrivals.
The monk Xuanjian of Nanzhao was long renowned for his clarity in the teachings and contemplation (*jiaoguan*), and was eloquent and erudite.
Yingfa said every day, "I have heard that the Great Tang possesses the Chan school. If it is indeed as such, I shall follow its teachings;
if it is not appropriate, I shall change its tenets and cause them to pursue the doctrinal teachings and contemplative practices.

Upon arriving from his country, he heard the Master’s words and immediately realized his former errors, gaining profound insight into the Great Dharma. He was just beginning to plan his return to propagate the Way when he passed away.
Zhongwu was a disciple of Guo’an. When he painted an image of his master and returned to his own country, the image emitted a divine light that illuminated the heavens.
Consequently, Nanzhao changed its teachings to Chan and honored the Master as the first patriarch of the Chan school. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Looking ahead, he is before you;
turning back, he is behind you. The bamboo-bird cries by day; the golden dragon roars at night. For those who have not yet understood, listen to one word: now, who is moving their mouth?"
The Preface states: "The sigh of 're-reading it three times'—a single drop of water can rival the vast ocean. Yao Fengqian said:
"Sui-ren rubbed fire to cook food for the offerings to the Supreme Deity; yet the First Emperor Qin used it to burn ancient books and scriptures.

The fifty-seventh patriarch, Chan Master Qianyan Yuanchang, was born in Tiaoshan of Yue to the Dong family. His family’s hereditary occupation was poetry and the classics. His father was Jiuding and his mother was née He.
When the Master was late in being born, his parents wished to abandon him; he was raised by his paternal aunt, née Xie. At the age of seven, he attended an external tutor;
upon seeing any book, he could recite it from memory. Whether entering or leaving, he walked with the measured gait of an adult. His father was delighted.

He said, "This boy shall uphold my lineage through his literary talent and conduct. His paternal uncles, Tan and Fang, studied Buddhism at Famen Yuan in Fuyang and requested the Master to accept him as a successor;
the Master declined and would not consent. Not long after, the Master fell gravely ill.
Xie prayed to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, saying, "May the Buddha have compassion for me and grant that this child does not die; let him serve as a menial attendant for the rest of his life."
After he had finished his prayers, the Master broke into a sweat and was cured. He then allowed [the boy] to follow him in his travels. At that time, the boy was seventeen years old;

he sought out excellent teachers and friends to sharpen his understanding through the rigorous study of the doctrines of the nine schools and the hundred masters. After some time, he remarked, "This is not the Dharma for transcending the world.

He then returned to his scripture teacher to study the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Upon reaching the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," he asked: "Since Bhaiṣajyarāja has already offered up both arms," [he continued].
"Why did he manifest his original body again? His bestowal of the sutras was extraordinary. At the age of nineteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He traveled to Wulin to study the Vinaya under a Vinaya Master at Lingzhi Temple. [The Master] asked him: "In the eightfold interactions of daily life, there is not the slightest discordance."

"What do you mean? the Master asked. The Vinaya Master said, "Why not ask about the ninth dharma? The Master replied, "He asks about the Vinaya, yet you answer with Chan; he is truly a vessel for the Mahayana Dharma.
Later, when the Chancellor Huìxíng held a meal for the monastic community at his residence, the Master entered among the assembly.

Tiānmù Běn was also seated there; seeing the Master from afar, he immediately called out to him, saying, "How is your daily practice? The Master replied, "I do nothing but recite [the Buddha's name]."

"Master Fu. Ben asked, "Where is the Buddha now? As the Master was about to offer a reply, Ben rebuked him with a stern voice. The Master then knelt on his right knee in homage and requested instruction on the essentials of the Dharma.
Ben bestowed upon him the "Puppy Has No Buddha-Nature" koan. Subsequently, the Master went to Mount Lingyin to live among the thatched huts.
Xueting summoned him to serve as the Director of Records (*neiji*). When the Master took up his pen, his compositions were complete and elegant, adorned with the five colors.
His brilliance was radiant; those who saw him marveled and submitted to his excellence. Suddenly, he abandoned [his studies] and returned home.
Nearly ten years passed until one day, he sighed deeply and said, "Throughout my life, my spirit and ambitions have filled the heavens and the earth; how can I now become a vinegar-worm in a jar?

He went back to Lingyin for three years, and while traveling to Wangting, he attained realization upon hearing the cry of a magpie. He hurried to see Benchou to recount this, but Benchou again rebuked him. The Master was filled with indignation.
He returned home. As night was falling into silence, a mouse suddenly overturned the cat’s food bowl; as it hit the ground, it made a sound. Suddenly, he attained enlightenment.
He put on his robes and waited for dawn, then went again to question his teacher, Ben. Ben asked, "Why did Zhaozhou say 'no'? The Master replied, "The mouse ate the cat's food.
Ben said, "Not yet. The Master said, "The food bowl is broken. Ben asked, "What after it is broken? The Master—
He said, "When the square bricks are built and crushed, my original intent will be revealed through a smile. Look at the Master and say: 'You should well protect and uphold yourself.
When the time for seclusion in mountain caves arrives, the principle will manifest of itself. Having received this entrustment, the Master hid himself in the eastern hermitage of Tianlong Shan.
His reputation and brilliance grew daily more prominent, and various famous mountains vied with one another to invite him. The Master, together with his disciple Xisheng, took up his staff and..."

Crossing the Tāng River, he traveled east to Mount Fúlóng in Wūshāng. Seeing that the mountain’s shape resembled a blue lotus flower, he planted his mendicant’s staff at the edge of a cliff and made a vow, saying:
"If there is water in this mountain, I shall dwell here. Suddenly, a mountain spring overflowed, appearing the color of white milk.
The Master then took up residence beneath a great tree. Originally, there was a Chan temple on Mount Fúlóng named Shèngshòu.

It had been abandoned for a long time. When the Master entered the mountains, the local villagers all dreamed that a strange monk had arrived. They then led one another up the steep crags and through the thick undergrowth to seek him out.
The Master sat in meditation, unmoving. The prominent families of the district each cut timber to construct a refined hermitage to provide shelter for the Master.
Subsequently, they built a great monastery based on his former name, featuring multi-storied pavilions, magnificent halls, and a grand main gate.

His fame shone forth, illuminating the forests and valleys. From within the borders—Qi, Lu, Yan, Zhao, Qin, Long, Min, and Shu—to the regions beyond—Japan, the Three Han, the Eight Fan, Luo Dian, Jiaozhi, and Ryūkyū—all rushed to prostrate themselves in worship and sought instruction in the study of the mind.

Those who remained numbered several hundred at all times. There were even those whose longing for the Way was so intense that they severed their own arms before the Master to demonstrate their resolve. The Master...
He preaches the Dharma for each according to their individual capacities. [He] ascends the hall and says: "Expensively purchasing rice from Luling, making it into large iron dumplings;
he invites all you Zen practitioners to swallow and devour them within the hall. Hehehe! This is merely a token of my sincere hospitality."
"Do not disdain its coldness.
Biao said, "The Bodhisattva of Great Compassion has a thousand-handed great man; who does not have one?
Yao Feng Qian said, "The distant mountains all join him in his voice."
The fifty-eighth patriarch was Chan Master Shiwu Shiwei of Wanfeng in Suzhou. He was the son of the Jin family of Leqing, Wenzhou; his mother’s surname was Zheng.
She dreamed that two figures, one a Confucian and one a Buddhist, entered her chamber, and upon waking, she gave birth to two sons.

The Master was the younger. A light illuminated the room at his birth, and Zheng, fearing this omen, wished to abandon him. His grandmother raised him instead. Even as an infant, whenever he saw a monk, he would immediately smile and join his palms in reverence.
His parents could not keep him from leaving the household life. He sent Li Yue to become a monk under Master Sheng, the lecturer at Yongqing Temple;

he was eleven years old at the time. He had previously been reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, and upon reaching the passage, "All dharmas, from their very origin, are by nature eternally quiescent and extinguished," he attained a profound realization.
He attained a state where empty space was pulverized and the great earth sank flat; it was beyond comparison with any worldly realm.
He subsequently went to Hangzhou to receive full ordination and visited Chan Master Zhiyan at Hupao. Zhiyan instructed him with the words of Nanquan regarding the "Three Not-sos.
Thereupon, he entered Mount Dapeng and established a hermitage on the ruins of Foji Temple, where he investigated the truth day and night until he forgot to sleep.
While eating one day, he heard the Abbot Master Zong discuss the story of Muzhou kicking over the water pitcher at Guishan.
He suddenly attained awakening and said, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. *Du!* This dullard deserves thirty blows!
Hearing of the spiritual reputation of Master Qianyan, he set out on foot for Fulong. When Qianyan ascended the hall, he cited the verse regarding the lotus leaf in a windless breeze.

As he moved, it was certain that fish were swimming. The Master came forth, let out a thunderous shout, and shook his sleeves to depart. Yunyan then descended from his seat and requested the Master to occupy the first seat.
Before long, the Master bestowed upon him the robe and verse. Initially, he resided at Mount Song on Lanxi; later, he moved to Wanfeng in Suzhou.
One day, as he ascended the hall, he opened both hands and said: "The gate of skillful means is wide open; please enter through it."
"Enter here. He then clenched both fists and said, "The secure barrier is closed; let us speak of matters within the home. Then he asked, "If it is neither opened nor closed, what then?
After a long silence, he gathered his *saṃghāṭī* robe and descended from the seat.

The sixtieth patriarch, Chan Master Dongming Huixia, at the age of fourteen, paid respects to Zhanran of Miaojue Temple in Danyang, where he left the household life and received full ordination.

Later, he traveled extensively to visit various masters throughout the land. Finally, he arrived at the place of Master Song in Yunjian; although he gained some insight into his primary object of study, the master would not grant him approval.
Huixia vowed that he would not cease until he had attained thorough realization. Consequently, for six days and nights, he remained in meditative concentration.
One night, he happened to emerge from meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Raising his head, he beheld a tall pine tree and experienced a sudden, expansive realization (*satori*).
He subsequently traveled to Xuanmu in Suzhou, where he met Master Guolín; their minds met like a needle and its eye. Guolín further introduced him to Master Bǎozàngchí.

He was dismissed from his duties and subsequently presented this verse: "A single punch shatters the vast void; The billions of Sumeru mountains leave no trace.
