Having served him for a very long time, he fully attained the Way and received formal certification (*in'ga*). He then lived in seclusion at Gu Dao Mountain in Anxi, Hangzhou.
For thirty years, his shadow did not leave the mountains. His lofty reputation spread far and wide, and practitioners from all quarters flocked to him;

eminent masters from every region vied to seek instruction at his feet. The Master exhorted them with tireless diligence, and there was none who, upon hearing even a single word, did not experience a clear and refreshing awakening.

Not long after, he moved to Jingci Monastery in Hunan, where his Way flourished even more greatly. On the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month in the year of Xinyou, he suddenly commanded his attendant:

The monks inventoried his belongings throughout his life and held a formal auction to provide a meal for the assembly. The entire community knew that the Master had no intention of remaining in this world and requested that he leave behind a verse of farewell.
The Master smiled and said, "I have a few idle words, but there is no one to whom they are addressed. On the twenty-ninth day, at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), he passed away.
He took leave of the assembly and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. His remains were kept in the reliquary for seven days; his countenance remained as if alive.
He was cremated according to the Dharma, and countless śarīras were obtained, brilliant and lustrous like pearls.
The inscription reads: "Pity those who race about the world; six times six is originally thirty-six. Yao Fengqian remarked:
"Who cares whether the months are large or small, or whether there are leap years?"
The sixty-first patriarch was Chan Master Yongci of Dongshan in Jinling. His secular surname was Yu, and he hailed from a prominent clan in Chengdu County in Shu.
From his childhood, he took delight in the tracks of monks; thus, he renounced the secular life and proceeded to Jingde Chan Temple on Mount Daisui in Peng County.
He went to Duzhao Yuegong to receive the tonsure; when Yue was in seclusion, the Master completed his duties at the Xiang Pagoda and entered the Western Mountains for eight years.
For the first time on his pilgrimage, he relied upon Master Taichu. One day, [Taichu] asked, "Before your parents were born, what was that which is your original face?
The Master walked from east to west and stood with his hands folded. Later, he left the gorges and traveled to the capital, where he received his official certificate. He returned...
He returned to Linggu Monastery in Jinling and took up residence there. Xuefeng Wuxin invited him to serve as the head seat (*śrāmaṇera*).
He composed commentaries on the Vinaya and traveled to Wulin to receive full ordination. Later, under Master Dongming Zhixian, he attained awakening beneath two blows of the master’s staff.

He then unfolded his sitting cloth, performed three prostrations with deep respect, and departed. Zhixian said, "I have lived at Gudao Mountain for thirty years, but today I have finally seen this monk."
Baizhang said, "As for us śramaṇas, at all times and in all places, we do not attend to the hands and feet of others' households.
Yao Feng Qian remarked, "There is a turning word; is there anyone who can answer it?"
The sixty-second patriarch, Zen Master Zhixuan of Gaogong Peak in Jinling, long relied upon Master Haizhou of Dongshan.
At the end, he was entrusted with the seal of the True Dharma and received the prediction: "Whether killing or giving life, whatever is brought forth is entirely manifest.
When Benrui came to visit him, the Master asked, "Where are you from? Rui replied, "Sichuan. The Master held up his fist and said, "Is there anything like this in Sichuan?"
"What is it? Cui replied, "There is none. The Master asked, "Why then is there none? Cui said, "It is not my realm.
The Master asked, "What, then, is your realm? Cui said, "Even the Buddhas cannot know it; who would dare to force a name upon it?
The Master said, "Are you not then clinging to emptiness? Cui said, "I certainly will not make my livelihood inside a ghost cave. The Master said, "In India..."
"Of the ninety-six kinds [of heterodox paths], you shall be the foremost.
Baotiao said, "Within the land of the Great Tang, there is one person who proclaims the Dharma-door of the Patriarchal Vehicle; all people on earth lose their very lives [in its presence].
Yao Feng Qian said, "From morning until evening, people speak by the thousands and tens of thousands, yet it is not that they do not speak."
The sixty-third patriarch was Chan Master Benrui of Jinling, a native of the Jiang family from Zhongling, Nanchang. Accompanying his father on a merchant journey to Yingzhou,
he happened to grow weary of worldly phenomena and, taking a casual stroll, arrived at Jingmen, where he paid respects to Master Wushuo Neng and received the tonsure and ordination.
He became a śramaṇa and was instructed to contemplate the saying, "The myriad dharmas return to one. He then traveled extensively to consult with senior masters.
Accompanying the head seat Quan, he reached Xiangyang. Along the way, they happened to hear an old woman calling her pig.
Quan spoke a verse, saying: "The mother calls 'Na-na' within the wall; Do the monks on the road understand? If you can break through this pivotal mechanism, [Then you will realize it.]”

The daughter remained as the mother-in-law; the Master’s doubts increased all the more. One day, while ill, he heard a monk cite the circumstances of Dahui’s passing, whereupon he suddenly clarified the meaning of Quan Gong’s verse.
He traveled to Sichuan to see the elders of Fushan and Xuefeng, from whom he received much medicinal instruction, causing his realization of the profound mysteries to reach even greater heights.
Finally, he met with the Venerable Gaofeng of Jinling; their interaction was characterized by an unyielding, horizontal engagement, as [Gaofeng] swept away [his remaining attachments].
Xiu went out through the sleeves; Xuan patted him and stamped his seal upon him.

The sixty-fourth patriarch was Chan Master Yuquan Mingcong, a native of Guanzhe County in Shaowu. His secular surname was Xi, and his mother was Lady Wu.
On the eve of the Master’s birth, a sick monk requested lodging; Lady Wu declined him, yet at midnight she gave birth to the Master.

He was diligent in the Vinaya and concurrently cultivated *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight). He conducted a profound study of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other treatises.

The sixty-fifth patriarch, Chan Master Yuantong Debao, was the son of the Wu family of Jintai Jin’i. Orphaned at a young age, his disposition and character were naturally inclined toward the Way.
